Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Delhi ahead of the 10 October protest. The order remains unpublished, and the police communication conveying it is marked "Top Secret".

9 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the internet shutdown imposed in parts of Delhi ahead of the protest called for tomorrow, 10 October 2026, at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner. A communication dated 9 October 2026 from the Deputy Commissioner of Police, Special Cell (HQ), Delhi to the nodal officers of Airtel, Vodafone Idea, Jio and MTNL, shared by the news agency ANI, records that the Union Home Secretary has authorised, on the request of the Delhi Police, the suspension of "mobile internet services (all technologies)" within a radius of four kilometres of the Janpath-Kartavya Path crossing, from 10 pm on 9 October to 10 pm on 10 October 2026. It refers to order No. 22016/12/2019-CIS-IV dated 9 October 2026 and is marked "Top Secret" at the top and bottom of the page.

As per a media report by Live Law, the Solicitor General informed the Supreme Court today that the shutdown is confined to "certain sensitive pockets" and will be reviewed on the basis of security inputs. The communication describes a circle of about 50 square kilometres across the centre of the capital, which takes in Jantar Mantar, Connaught Place, India Gate, Parliament, the Supreme Court, the Delhi High Court, New Delhi Railway Station and hospitals including Ram Manohar Lohia and Lady Hardinge. This is about seven times the area of the suspension ordered around Jantar Mantar on 2 October, and it runs for twice as long.

Delhi Police has refused permission for the protest, and prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force in New Delhi district. Delhi Police asked for the gates of 57 metro stations to be closed from 9 pm today, and the Railways cancelled trains due at New Delhi and Hazrat Nizamuddin between 4 am and 2 pm tomorrow. Hearing a challenge to these measures today, the Supreme Court directed that there be no complete prohibition on metro and train services and asked the authorities to keep in mind the principle of proportionality. As reported, that order did not examine the internet shutdown. We call for the order to be withdrawn, and for mobile internet to remain available across Delhi tomorrow.

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public knows the area and hours of this shutdown from a police communication marked "Top Secret" that was shared by ANI, and not from the government. That communication records no reasons, and the order of the Union Home Secretary to which it refers has not been made public. This is now a pattern and the order for the shutdown of 2 October around Jantar Mantar became public four days later, when the Hindu obtained a copy.

This secrecy is contrary to the law declared by the Supreme Court. In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Court held that "an order, particularly one that affects lives, liberty and property of people, must be made available". It directed the authorities to "publish all orders in force and any future orders" suspending telecom services, including the internet, "to enable the affected persons to challenge it before the High Court or appropriate forum". A democracy "sworn to transparency and accountability", the Court said, "necessarily mandates the production of orders as it is the right of an individual to know". The Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, framed under Section 20 of the Telecommunications Act, 2023, now provide that every suspension order "shall be published", must state its reasons, and must be limited to a clearly defined geographical area and a specified duration. No order may be made unless the authority has considered that its objectives cannot be achieved by any other reasonable means.

The communication shared by ANI invokes Rule 3 of these Rules, the same Rule that requires the order to be published. It is nevertheless marked "Top Secret", the highest security classification used by the Government of India. In January 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs issued orders bearing the same number to suspend the internet at Singhu, Ghazipur and Tikri during the farmers' protest, and those orders remain available on the Ministry's own website. An order cannot be published and kept "Top Secret" at the same time.

The government has placed no evidence before the public that a shutdown makes a protest safer. The available research is to the contrary as a 2019 study of shutdowns and protest in India by Jan Rydzak, then at Stanford's Global Digital Policy Incubator, found shutdowns "much more strongly associated with increases in violent collective action than with non-violent mobilization". The Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights reported in 2022 that many shutdowns justified on grounds of public safety or national security "were followed by spikes in violence" (A/HRC/50/55). In December 2021, the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Communications and Information Technology recorded that neither the Department of Telecommunications nor the Ministry of Home Affairs had studied the impact of shutdowns.

A shutdown also prevents people from documenting and reporting what happens at a protest. The same UN report found that, “the inability to access tools to document and rapidly report abuses seems to contribute to further violence”. Without mobile internet, a journalist at Jantar Mantar cannot file her report or broadcast live. A protester cannot upload a video as events unfold, and a person who is injured or detained cannot send a location to family or a lawyer. On 20 July 2026, mobile internet in Central Delhi was switched off amid reports of the use of force to disperse protesters. In Manipur in 2023, video of an assault on two women on 4 May reached the public only on 19 July, while a shutdown imposed on 3 May was still in force. This is the impact an internet shutdown has which rather than preventing violence prevents the documentation of illegality.

Our demands:

We call upon the Ministry of Home Affairs and the Delhi Police to:
1) Withdraw order No. 22016/12/2019-CIS-IV dated 9 October 2026 and keep mobile internet services running across Delhi on 10 October 2026.
2) Publish that order, and every other suspension order issued in connection with the protest, forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.
3) Withdraw the "Top Secret" marking, and stop classifying suspension orders and the communications that convey them to telecom operators.
4) Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and publish its final order, as the Supreme Court required on 23 February 2024.
5) Ensure that journalists and members of the public can record and report from the protest sites without obstruction.

text:
Poland is in the middle of a sharp standoff over its Constitutional Tribunal. On Friday, October 30, Judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska announced a one-month suspension of the Tribunal's president, Bogdan Święczkowski, and his deputy, Bartłomiej Sochański, effectively taking control of the court. Police surrounded the building but did not enter. The court's website went down, and the Tribunal itself called the move an "illegal takeover" and a "coup d'état." Protesters gathered outside, and three were detained.
President Karol Nawrocki cut short a trip to Senegal and flew back to Warsaw. He is due to consult the president of the Supreme Court.
The conflict goes back to 2015, when Law and Justice (PiS) took political control of the Tribunal. In December 2025, the EU's top court ruled that the Tribunal is not independent and impartial. Tusk's government, which came to power in 2023 promising to restore judicial independence, says Święczkowski was blocking legally elected judges from working. The president refused to swear in three of the six judges elected by the Sejm in 2026, and Święczkowski has kept Sejm-elected judges out of hearings.
The sides. Tusk says restoring the rule of law "requires decisive action." Sikorski says the president and the Tribunal's leadership were preventing the elected majority from working, so action was necessary. Kaczyński says Poland is becoming a "police state," Ziobro calls for resistance, and PiS-aligned MEPs call it a coup. Poland's ambassador to China, Jakub Kumoch, resigned over the events.
The situation is moving fast. The legal status of the suspension is disputed, and the next steps by the president and the Supreme Court are not yet known.

text:
PUBLIC STATEMENT BY PARANJOY GUHA THAKURTA
On the arbitrary takedown of https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe by Hostinger following legal notices from Indiabulls founder Sameer Gehlaut
October 31, 2026
On the morning of October 28, 2026, my website https://t.co/OeAAoTPXCy and all its associated subdomains, including https://t.co/I8kylhDXVk and https://t.co/D8b6LtNzWD, were abruptly taken offline by our web hosting provider, Hostinger (HOSTINGER operations, UAB). The website, registered twelve years ago, serves as an online archive of my work over several decades as a journalist, author, publisher, and maker of documentary films and music videos
Hostinger gave no prior intimation, warning, or opportunity to respond before suspending the entire hosting account. When my colleague contacted Hostinger “Support” at 6:48 AM on October 28, a hosting “specialist” stated that the suspension was triggered by an abuse report for "Fraud/Scam" and declared that "unsuspension is not negotiable in this case."
This sudden shutdown of an entire repository under the label "Fraud/Scam" happened just days after Sameer Gehlaut, founder of the Indiabulls group, served me with an ex parte court order demanding the removal of a single article published more than seven years on https://t.co/25noyNupwJ.
For over six years, Indiabulls and Shri Gehlaut have pursued legal action over this report and I have consistently defended our journalistic report in court. Here is the timeline:
·  March 11, 2020: Indiabulls Housing Finance Limited filed a criminal defamation complaint (CC No. 1765/2020) before the Patiala House Courts, New Delhi, against NewsClick, its Reader's Editor Urmilesh, co-author of the article Sourodipto Sanyal, NewsClick editor Prabir Purkayastha, and me over an article published on the website on September 30, 2019.
·  June 6, 2025 and July 9, 2025: More than five years after the complaint was filed, a Judicial Magistrate at Patiala House Courts passed an order on June 6, 2025, dropping proceedings against Shri Purkayastha while issuing summons to the remaining four accused, including me, under Sections 499 and 500 of the Indian Penal Code. A formal summons was issued on July 9, 2025, for appearance on July 30, 2025.
·  August 27, 2026: Counsel for Shri Gehlaut, sent me a legal notice demanding the takedown of the article within 24 to 48 hours, claiming that a status report by the Economic Offences Wing (EOW) of the Delhi Police had altered the factual position.
·  September 2, 2026: My counsel sent a reply pointing out concerns with the legal notice
·  October 24, 2026: Indiabulls Nests Limited (Plaintiff No. 1) and Sameer Gehlaut (Plaintiff No. 2) obtained an ex parte ad interim injunction from the Court of one of the District and Sessions Judges, Patiala House Courts, New Delhi, in Civil Suit No. 529/2026 (Indiabulls Nests Ltd. & Anr. v. Ashok Kumar/John Doe & Ors.), in which I am arrayed as Defendant No. 19. The order directed the removal and de-indexing of the article on https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe (listed as Item A-33 in Schedule A).
·  October 25, 2026 (10:13 AM IST): Advocates representing Indiabulls Nests Limited and Sameer Gehlaut, emailed me the October 24 court order and suit documents, demanding immediate deletion and written confirmation of compliance.
·  October 26, 2026 (11:33 PM IST): Sameer Gehlaut personally sent an email from his official address (sameer@indiabulls.com) demanding the immediate deletion of the URL from https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe and threatening to move the court under Order XXXIX Rule 2A of the Code of Civil Procedure if I did not comply, noting that the matter is next listed on December 18, 2026. While I was in the process of challenging the order dated 24.10.2026 before higher forums, on the same day, advocates representing Shri Gehlaut submitted a court order takedown complaint to Google LLC.

·  October 28, 2026 (3:16 PM IST): Google Search Console sent an automated notice ([WNC-598900]) informing me that Google was blocking the specific URL https://t.co/SsSVUVLKGX  from appearing in search results on https://t.co/2IOZ4I1WqC.

The Lumen Database record of this complaint (Notice ID: 101001876) reveals the scale of the takedown request. The complaint targeted 52 URLs on websites across major national and international news organisations, including The Economic Times, Business Standard, The Caravan, The Daily Pioneer, Business Today, Deccan Herald, ET Now, Financial Express, Livemint, Moneycontrol, Moneylife, NDTV Profit, The New Indian Express, Outlook Business, The Quint, Quartz, and NewsClick, along with posts on X (formerly Twitter), Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, and Scribd.

Most of these reports on major corporate news websites remain accessible online. In fact, Item 39 on the Lumen takedown list is the original September 30, 2019 article published on https://t.co/qQP2N2fxA2: https://t.co/hgneAPvDuF, which remains live and accessible  as of now.

Yet, in the case of https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe, the entire domain and every website hosted on my account were wiped off the internet.

Hostinger's Baseless "Fraud/Scam" Claim and Demand for Accountability

Hostinger did not cite the Patiala House Courts order when it suspended my account on October 28, 2026. Instead, its representative claimed that the hosting account was permanently suspended due to an abuse report for "Fraud/Scam".

This allegation is demonstrably false:

1. VirusTotal Security Analysis: Independent domain checks conducted on October 28, 2026, at 7:48 AM and 7:54 AM on VirusTotal confirm that 0 out of 92 security vendors flagged https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe or https://t.co/I8kylhDXVk as malicious, phishing, or fraudulent. VirusTotal explicitly categorises https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe under "news and media".

2. Google Safe Browsing Status: Checks on the Google Safe Browsing diagnostic tool at 7:55 AM and 7:56 AM on October 28, 2026, for both https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe and https://t.co/D8b6LtNzWD returned the status: "No unsafe content found".
My website https://t.co/OeAAoTPXCy does not sell financial products, solicit funds for commercial schemes, or engage in any activity that could remotely be classified as a scam. It is a repository of public-interest journalism, books, documentary films, and investigative reports built over a lifetime of work. By acting on a fabricated "Fraud/Scam" abuse report without a single verification check or prior notice to the domain owner, Hostinger has allowed its abuse-reporting mechanism to be weaponised to censor an independent journalist.
Even where a court order directs the removal or de-indexing of a specific URL, a web hosting provider has no legal or ethical justification to pull down an entire domain and hundreds of unrelated articles, archives, and subdomains without notice.
I demand immediate answers and accountability from Hostinger:
1. Who submitted the false "Fraud/Scam" abuse report against https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe, and on what exact date and time was it received?
2. What internal verification did Hostinger's abuse team conduct before classifying a 12-year-old journalism portal as a "Fraud/Scam" site, especially when 92 security vendors on VirusTotal and Google Safe Browsing show zero malicious or unsafe content?
3. Why was no prior notice, warning, or copy of the complaint sent to me before suspending the entire hosting account?
4. On what basis did Hostinger's specialist declare that the suspension of an entire archive of journalistic work is "not negotiable"?
While my legal advisers are in the process of taking appropriate steps in court regarding the ex parte order dated October 24, 2026, and the wholesale suspension of my website, this backdoor censorship through web hosting providers sets a dangerous precedent for the independence of the media and freedom of expression as enshrined in Article (19)(1)(a) of the Constitution of India as a fundamental right of every citizen of India.
Yours sincerely

Paranjoy Guha Thakurta
Independent Journalist, Author, Publisher and Maker of Documentary Films and Music Videos

Before you post, you need to know if they can actually get your video taken down for speaking your truth."

[Do Not Skip This Part]👇
Note: This tweet is only for general understanding of how this happens. A recent tracking down of a video involving the brand has occurred. Here is a thread to understand how it happens. Please refrain from mentioning the brand name or creator name in comments or replies to this tweet. 
 
In India, there is no simple rule allowing a brand to remove a video simply because it criticizes the brand. 

The usual route is a mix of:

IT Act + IT Rules + platform policy + civil court injunction/defamation/commercial disparagement suit.

1) What is the core legal structure?

Platforms like YouTube, X, Instagram, etc. are treated as intermediaries. They get “safe harbor” protection for user-generated content, but they may lose that protection if they ignore valid legal directions.

Under India’s intermediary framework, a platform gets legally strong “actual knowledge” mainly through:

A court order, or
A government/authorized agency direction/intimation

A private brand complaint alone usually does not automatically force a platform to remove a video. 

The Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India - clarified that platforms should not be forced to decide legality merely based on private complaints; the stronger trigger is a court order or government direction.

2) How does a brand complaint become a court order?

The structure usually works like this:

Step 1: The brand's legal team collects evidence

The company gathers the video URL, transcript, screenshots, claims made in the video, alleged false statements, impact on reputation, possible business loss, and proof of harm.

Step 2: The brand's legal team may send a legal notice

This is often the first pressure step. The brand may demand a takedown, an apology, a correction, damages, or the removal of specific claims.

Step 3: The brand files a civil/commercial suit.

If the creator does not comply, the brand can file a case for defamation, commercial disparagement, trademark issues, unfair trade practice, or reputational/business harm.

Step 4: The brand asks for urgent interim relief

The brand may request an interim injunction, sometimes ex parte, meaning the court can issue a temporary order without first hearing the creator if it believes urgent harm may occur.

Step 5: The court checks the matter prima facie

At this stage, the court is not finally deciding who is right. It checks whether there is an arguable case that the content may be false, misleading, malicious, defamatory, or commercially disparaging.

Step 6: The court may pass an injunction

The order can direct the creator to remove the video, stop sharing it, stop repeating certain claims, or restrain publication of similar allegedly disparaging content.

Step 7: The court order is sent to the platform
Once YouTube/X/Instagram receives the order, the platform may remove or disable access to the video to comply and protect its intermediary safe harbor.

3) Does the brand need to contact the platform grievance officer?

They can, but for defamation or brand-disparagement disputes, the platform may not want to act purely on the brand’s private complaint unless the violation is very clear under platform policy.

The more powerful route is:

Brand → Court → Court order → Platform compliance

The grievance officer becomes important when the platform receives a complaint, legal notice, or court/government order. But the grievance officer is not usually the final judge of whether a review is defamatory or fair criticism.

4) Can a video be removed just because it criticizes a company?

No. Criticism alone should not be enough.

A creator can usually criticize a product, company, service, pricing, quality, privacy policy, design, marketing claims, or consumer experience.

But risk increases when the video makes strong factual claims, such as:

“this phone is fake”
“this company is cheating customers”
“this is just a rebranded phone”
“do not buy this because the company is lying”
“this brand is a scam”

These claims need proof. If the creator presents them as facts and the company says they are false, misleading, malicious, or damaging to business, the company may go to court.

5) What does the court usually look at?

For a temporary injunction, the court may consider:

Prima facie case: Is there an arguable case that the content is false, misleading, defamatory, or commercially disparaging?

Balance of convenience: Who will suffer more harm if the order is or is not granted?

Irreparable harm: Can the damage to reputation or business be fixed later with money, or is immediate restraint needed?

Proof and testing: Did the creator rely on reliable documents, technical tests, expert analysis, official sources, or only assumptions?

Language used: Was the tone fair and analytical, or aggressive and conclusive without enough proof?

6) What can the creator do after an ex parte order?

The creator can challenge the order in the same court. 

They can ask the court to vacate or modify the injunction and argue that:
the video was fair comment,
the claims were based on evidence,
the company suppressed facts,
the order was passed without hearing the creator,
the takedown is too broad,
or public interest requires the video to remain available.

7) Practical creator lesson

A review video is safer when it clearly separates:

Opinion: “In my view, this looks like poor value.”

Fact: “The model number matches X device.”

Evidence: screenshots, teardown, software logs, official filings, import data, product pages, privacy policy, benchmark/test method.

Limitations: “Based on my testing,” “I could not independently verify X,” “the brand has been contacted for comment.”

The danger zone is when the creator makes a strong factual allegation without showing a reliable testing method or source.

Important point:
Fair criticism is not illegal. But factual claims like “fake phone”, “rebranded phone”, “scam”, “company is cheating” need strong proof.

Disclaimer: I have shared only how the law is applied in such cases; this tweet does not reflect my opinion or view on any similar incident. 

Bookmark this for the future; this will be useful for a lot of creators out there.

मोदी जी द्वारा दिए गए कल डिजिटल मंचों और लोकतंत्र को लेकर अपने झूठे विचार रखे जिनकी पोल खुल चुकी है।
दिल्ली में पत्रकारों, यू ट्यूबर,सोशल मीडिया एक्टिविस्ट को पीटा गिरफ्तार किया गया, सोशल मीडिया एकाउंट बंद किए जा रहे है लगातार।

कंपनियां हर महीने भारत सरकार को अपनी 'मासिक अनुपालन रिपोर्ट' (Monthly Compliance Report) सौंपती हैं
Facebook और Instagram (Meta): मेटा ने भारत के अन्दर 6 महीनों में 1.6 लाख (160,000) से अधिक अकाउंट्स पर सीधे बड़ी कार्रवाई की है।
• ट्विटर (X एक्स: एक महीने की अवधि में ही भारत में 5 लाख से अधिक अकाउंट्स को पूरी तरह बैन किया है। जिनमें कुछ समाचार पोर्टल और पत्रकारों के हैंडल भी शामिल थे।

गृह मंत्रालय के 'सहयोग पोर्टल' (Sahyog Portal) और IT एक्ट की धाराओं के तहत मार्च से जुलाई 2026 के बीच करीब 1.95 लाख (195,000) कंटेंट ब्लॉकिंग और टेकडाउन आदेश जारी किए गए। यह औसतन हर 68 सेकंड में एक आदेश के बराबर है।
• Instagram: सबसे ज़्यादा लगभग 1 लाख (100,000) ब्लॉकिंग आदेश मिले।
• Facebook: करीब 80,000 टेकडाउन और ब्लॉकिंग निर्देश दिए गए。
• YouTube: लगभग 15,000 आदेश जारी किए गए।

प्रधानमंत्री नरेंद्र मोदी ने नई दिल्ली में आयोजित आठवें ब्लूमबर्ग न्यू इकोनॉमी फोरम (Bloomberg New Economy Forum) में देश के डिजिटल मंचों और लोकतंत्र को लेकर अपने विचार रखे।
उन्होंने भारत को 'लोकतंत्र की जननी' (Mother of Democracy) बताया और कहा कि भारत में 100 से अधिक भाषाएं, करीब 80,000 पंजीकृत समाचार पत्र और 1,000 से ज्यादा सैटेलाइट टीवी चैनल मौजूद हैं।
उन्होंने बताया कि भारत में 50 करोड़ से अधिक लोग यूट्यूब और 50 करोड़ से अधिक लोग इंस्टाग्राम का इस्तेमाल करते हैं, जो ऑनलाइन नागरिक चर्चाओं में सक्रिय रूप से भाग लेते हैं।
उन्होंने कहा कि इन डिजिटल मंचों ने एक ऐसा मंच तैयार किया है जहां नागरिक खुले तौर पर विचारों का आदान-प्रदान और राष्ट्रीय मुद्दों पर बहस करते हैं।

text:
MeitY's advisory to Meta directs the suppression of protest reporting on Instagram and Facebook. It must be withdrawn.

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

5. Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose on what inputs its "automated system" acts.

Any person whose account or content has been withheld in India since 8 October 2026 may write to IFF at legal@internetfreedom.in. IFF is providing assistance pro bono.

https://t.co/X7ipfsVLzu condemns arbitrary content and account restrictions faced by users on Meta platforms, X, and Reddit.

Over the past 20 days, https://t.co/X7ipfsVLzu’s Free Speech Tracker has recorded 200+ cases of content blocking and account restrictions on @Meta platforms, @X, and @Reddit. Many of the recently blocked posts were critical of the government, called for protests, featured journalists’ reporting, addressed ongoing issues, or even demanded justice in a murder case, among other topics. These restrictions are not only limited to feed posts, but Meta has also restricted Instagram Stories and comments online. https://t.co/X7ipfsVLzu has also recorded various instances of FIRs filed against users raising their voices online.

Those affected include stand-up comedians, journalists, digital media organisations, civil society organisations, cartoonists, meme pages, political representatives and other users. Out of these, https://t.co/X7ipfsVLzu has recorded 20+ independent journalists and digital media organisations who have faced restrictions, including @LiveLawIndia, @moliticsindia, and @4pmnews_network.

According to the publicly available information, the affected posts were restricted pursuant to the “legal requests” received by the platforms or through Meta’s automated systems. https://t.co/X7ipfsVLzu is deeply concerned about the increasing reliance on automated systems for implementing content restrictions and legal compliance requirements. https://t.co/X7ipfsVLzu emphasises that journalists and news outlets are facing systemic suppression due to over-automated content moderation systems that lack context for investigative reporting, public interest documentation, and critical commentary. By conflating legitimate reporting on sensitive or controversial issues with violations of Community Standards or legal requirements through automated moderation, Meta effectively silences public-interest journalism without human oversight.

In many cases, users are provided little or no meaningful explanation about the legal or factual basis of the restriction or what steps they can take to challenge the decision. Such opaque moderation practices undermine users’ ability to understand how platform policies are enforced and make it difficult to distinguish between legitimate moderation and arbitrary or inconsistent decision-making.

These issues are exacerbated by the lack of human review in the escalation process, with aggrieved users facing constant automated and AI-generated responses which often fail to address even the most apparent errors in moderation. Coupled with unresponsive and inefficient grievance officer reporting procedures, users are all but helpless.

https://t.co/X7ipfsVLzu has consistently advocated against these practices. We are concerned that these content and account restrictions are contrary to the rule of law and to India’s constitutional commitment to freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution.

In light of the above, https://t.co/X7ipfsVLzu calls upon Meta to restore https://t.co/X7ipfsVLzu’s post with immediate effect and provide a clear explanation of the legal basis for the takedown. Meta must also ensure meaningful human oversight for restrictions and provide users with an effective and timely mechanism to challenge erroneous takedowns, especially if done by automated systems. 

https://t.co/X7ipfsVLzu further calls upon the Government to provide greater transparency about the legal and policy basis for content restrictions and to clarify whether restrictions were imposed pursuant to government or law-enforcement requests or through Meta’s own systems. The Government should also ensure that the users are provided with meaningful, accessible, and timely avenues to contest takedowns.

Therefore, we sent all the required details to the same email address, including the content of our complaint filed with the GAC, along with all the supporting proof @googledrive links.

Despite this, we have now received an email stating that they cannot process our appeal.

When we checked the email to understand what information was required, we found only two or three points that needed to be addressed. We had already mentioned those three points and provided supporting evidence.

We provided proof of the content that was deleted, proof of where the content was saved, and an explanation of why our content should be restored. We also provided evidence explaining that the removal happened due to a mistake in the original report.

Despite providing all these details and supporting proofs, we have still received an email stating that Instagram cannot process our appeal.

For now, we are planning to wait and then reply again to the same ticket ID, clearly addressing those three points and providing the required information once more. We hope that our issue will be reviewed again and finally resolved.

In our next reply, @metaindia we will attach the original screenshots as proper evidence, hiding only certain details for privacy. This will help everyone understand that we are taking timely and proper action, providing the required information, and following the appropriate process.

But despite all our efforts, supporting evidence, and repeated attempts to resolve this matter, Instagram is still not restoring our removed content.

We will continue documenting every step and sharing updates with the relevant evidence so that everyone can see the actions we are taking to resolve this issue.

Rejection of Plaint and Return of Plaint: The Difference

Under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, rejection and return of a plaint are not the same. The distinction lies in the grounds for the order and its legal consequences.

Rejection of Plaint — Order VII Rule 11 CPC

A plaint may be rejected where:

It does not disclose a cause of action.
The relief is undervalued and the plaintiff fails to correct it within the time allowed.
The plaint is insufficiently stamped and the required court fee is not supplied within the time allowed.
The suit appears from the statements in the plaint to be barred by law.
The plaint is not filed in duplicate.
The plaintiff fails to comply with Order VII Rule 9 CPC.

Rejection of a plaint amounts to a decree under Section 2(2) CPC and is appealable under Section 96 CPC. Order VII Rule 13 also makes clear that rejection does not, by itself, bar the filing of a fresh plaint, subject to limitation and other legal requirements.

Return of Plaint — Order VII Rule 10 CPC

A plaint is returned when it is to be presented before the court in which the suit ought to have been instituted. This commonly arises where the court lacks territorial or pecuniary jurisdiction. Questions of subject-matter jurisdiction must be dealt with under the applicable law.

An order returning a plaint is appealable under Order XLIII Rule 1(a) CPC, subject to the applicable procedure, including Order VII Rule 10A where relevant.

The practical distinction is important: rejection is governed by Order VII Rule 11; return is governed by Order VII Rule 10. The applicable provision determines the nature of the order and the remedy available to the aggrieved party.

text:
Vijay and Nayanthara land in London for a 10-day film shoot.

While walking through crowded Oxford Street, professional pickpockets bump into them.
Neither feels a thing. Their metal credit cards are lifted clean out of their coats.

At 7:00 AM, both wake up to horror SMS alerts:
While they were asleep, someone tapped and swiped ₹17.56 Lakhs across luxury boutiques in Mayfair.
Zero OTP was received.

Both call their Indian bank in a panic. The support manager drops the hammer:
"International offline chip/tap transactions do not require Indian SMS OTPs. Pay the ₹17.56 Lakhs by the 20th, or 42% APR interest kicks in and your CIBIL score crashes 130 points."

Vijay panics, files a London police report, waits 4 months, and pays the entire ₹17.56 Lakh bill out of pocket from his savings to protect his credit score.
Nayanthara says 2 calm sentences.

7 days later, the bank credits 100% of the ₹17.56 Lakhs back, charges ₹0 in interest, and closes the case.

Same London street. Same stolen card. Same ₹17.56L fraud.

The only difference?↓

2. The Mandatory 10-Day "Shadow Credit" (Para 9)

Banks will tell you: "Pay the bill first. Wait 90 to 120 days for Visa/Mastercard arbitration."

This violates RBI regulations.
Under Para 9 of the RBI Master Direction:
The issuing bank is statutorily mandated to credit the full disputed amount ("Shadow Credit") back to the cardholder’s account within EXACTLY 10 working days of notification.

They cannot make you pay first or wait for their investigation.

Furthermore, under RBI mandates:
• The bank CANNOT levy interest, late fees, or finance charges on the disputed sum.
• The bank is strictly prohibited from reporting the unpaid disputed balance as an overdue default to CIBIL, Experian, or CRIF.

3. The "Burden of Proof" Checkmate (Para 12)

If the bank pushes back claiming "the physical card was swiped":

Quote Para 12 of the RBI circular directly:
"The burden of proving customer liability in unauthorised electronic banking transactions lies entirely on the bank."

The bank must furnish forensic proof or 2-factor authentication proving YOU authorized the transaction. They cannot.

If the branch stalls beyond 10 days, escalate instantly on the RBI CMS portal (cms .rbi .org .in) under the Integrated Ombudsman Scheme.
Banks face severe regulatory penalties for violating RBI Master Directions.

Within 48 hours of an Ombudsman filing, the bank clears the balance.

Vijay lost ₹17.56 Lakhs to bank panic.
Nayanthara paid ₹0 by triggering RBI's 10-day shadow credit rule.

Save this before your next international trip. You will need this one day.

On the arbitrary takedown of https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe by Hostinger following legal notices from Indiabulls founder Sameer Gehlaut
October 31, 2026
On the morning of October 28, 2026, my website https://t.co/OeAAoTPXCy and all its associated subdomains, including https://t.co/I8kylhDXVk and https://t.co/D8b6LtNzWD, were abruptly taken offline by our web hosting provider, Hostinger (HOSTINGER operations, UAB). The website, registered twelve years ago, serves as an online archive of my work over several decades as a journalist, author, publisher, and maker of documentary films and music videos
Hostinger gave no prior intimation, warning, or opportunity to respond before suspending the entire hosting account. When my colleague contacted Hostinger “Support” at 6:48 AM on October 28, a hosting “specialist” stated that the suspension was triggered by an abuse report for "Fraud/Scam" and declared that "unsuspension is not negotiable in this case."
This sudden shutdown of an entire repository under the label "Fraud/Scam" happened just days after Sameer Gehlaut, founder of the Indiabulls group, served me with an ex parte court order demanding the removal of a single article published more than seven years on https://t.co/25noyNupwJ.
For over six years, Indiabulls and Shri Gehlaut have pursued legal action over this report and I have consistently defended our journalistic report in court. Here is the timeline:
·  March 11, 2020: Indiabulls Housing Finance Limited filed a criminal defamation complaint (CC No. 1765/2020) before the Patiala House Courts, New Delhi, against NewsClick, its Reader's Editor Urmilesh, co-author of the article Sourodipto Sanyal, NewsClick editor Prabir Purkayastha, and me over an article published on the website on September 30, 2019.
·  June 6, 2025 and July 9, 2025: More than five years after the complaint was filed, a Judicial Magistrate at Patiala House Courts passed an order on June 6, 2025, dropping proceedings against Shri Purkayastha while issuing summons to the remaining four accused, including me, under Sections 499 and 500 of the Indian Penal Code. A formal summons was issued on July 9, 2025, for appearance on July 30, 2025.
·  August 27, 2026: Counsel for Shri Gehlaut, sent me a legal notice demanding the takedown of the article within 24 to 48 hours, claiming that a status report by the Economic Offences Wing (EOW) of the Delhi Police had altered the factual position.
·  September 2, 2026: My counsel sent a reply pointing out concerns with the legal notice
·  October 24, 2026: Indiabulls Nests Limited (Plaintiff No. 1) and Sameer Gehlaut (Plaintiff No. 2) obtained an ex parte ad interim injunction from the Court of one of the District and Sessions Judges, Patiala House Courts, New Delhi, in Civil Suit No. 529/2026 (Indiabulls Nests Ltd. & Anr. v. Ashok Kumar/John Doe & Ors.), in which I am arrayed as Defendant No. 19. The order directed the removal and de-indexing of the article on https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe (listed as Item A-33 in Schedule A).
·  October 25, 2026 (10:13 AM IST): Advocates representing Indiabulls Nests Limited and Sameer Gehlaut, emailed me the October 24 court order and suit documents, demanding immediate deletion and written confirmation of compliance.
·  October 26, 2026 (11:33 PM IST): Sameer Gehlaut personally sent an email from his official address (sameer@indiabulls.com) demanding the immediate deletion of the URL from https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe and threatening to move the court under Order XXXIX Rule 2A of the Code of Civil Procedure if I did not comply, noting that the matter is next listed on December 18, 2026. While I was in the process of challenging the order dated 24.10.2026 before higher forums, on the same day, advocates representing Shri Gehlaut submitted a court order takedown complaint to Google LLC.

·  October 28, 2026 (3:16 PM IST): Google Search Console sent an automated notice ([WNC-598900]) informing me that Google was blocking the specific URL https://t.co/SsSVUVLKGX  from appearing in search results on https://t.co/2IOZ4I1WqC.

The Lumen Database record of this complaint (Notice ID: 101001876) reveals the scale of the takedown request. The complaint targeted 52 URLs on websites across major national and international news organisations, including The Economic Times, Business Standard, The Caravan, The Daily Pioneer, Business Today, Deccan Herald, ET Now, Financial Express, Livemint, Moneycontrol, Moneylife, NDTV Profit, The New Indian Express, Outlook Business, The Quint, Quartz, and NewsClick, along with posts on X (formerly Twitter), Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, and Scribd.

Most of these reports on major corporate news websites remain accessible online. In fact, Item 39 on the Lumen takedown list is the original September 30, 2019 article published on https://t.co/qQP2N2fxA2: https://t.co/hgneAPvDuF, which remains live and accessible  as of now.

Yet, in the case of https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe, the entire domain and every website hosted on my account were wiped off the internet.

Hostinger's Baseless "Fraud/Scam" Claim and Demand for Accountability

Hostinger did not cite the Patiala House Courts order when it suspended my account on October 28, 2026. Instead, its representative claimed that the hosting account was permanently suspended due to an abuse report for "Fraud/Scam".

This allegation is demonstrably false:

1. VirusTotal Security Analysis: Independent domain checks conducted on October 28, 2026, at 7:48 AM and 7:54 AM on VirusTotal confirm that 0 out of 92 security vendors flagged https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe or https://t.co/I8kylhDXVk as malicious, phishing, or fraudulent. VirusTotal explicitly categorises https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe under "news and media".

2. Google Safe Browsing Status: Checks on the Google Safe Browsing diagnostic tool at 7:55 AM and 7:56 AM on October 28, 2026, for both https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe and https://t.co/D8b6LtNzWD returned the status: "No unsafe content found".
My website https://t.co/OeAAoTPXCy does not sell financial products, solicit funds for commercial schemes, or engage in any activity that could remotely be classified as a scam. It is a repository of public-interest journalism, books, documentary films, and investigative reports built over a lifetime of work. By acting on a fabricated "Fraud/Scam" abuse report without a single verification check or prior notice to the domain owner, Hostinger has allowed its abuse-reporting mechanism to be weaponised to censor an independent journalist.
Even where a court order directs the removal or de-indexing of a specific URL, a web hosting provider has no legal or ethical justification to pull down an entire domain and hundreds of unrelated articles, archives, and subdomains without notice.
I demand immediate answers and accountability from Hostinger:
1. Who submitted the false "Fraud/Scam" abuse report against https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe, and on what exact date and time was it received?
2. What internal verification did Hostinger's abuse team conduct before classifying a 12-year-old journalism portal as a "Fraud/Scam" site, especially when 92 security vendors on VirusTotal and Google Safe Browsing show zero malicious or unsafe content?
3. Why was no prior notice, warning, or copy of the complaint sent to me before suspending the entire hosting account?
4. On what basis did Hostinger's specialist declare that the suspension of an entire archive of journalistic work is "not negotiable"?
While my legal advisers are in the process of taking appropriate steps in court regarding the ex parte order dated October 24, 2026, and the wholesale suspension of my website, this backdoor censorship through web hosting providers sets a dangerous precedent for the independence of the media and freedom of expression as enshrined in Article (19)(1)(a) of the Constitution of India as a fundamental right of every citizen of India.
Yours sincerely

Paranjoy Guha Thakurta
Independent Journalist, Author, Publisher and Maker of Documentary Films and Music Videos

WHY ARE SOCIAL MEDIA TAKEDOWNS IN FOCUS?

Introduction

Increasing content takedowns expose the tension between digital governance and constitutional freedoms, raising concerns over censorship, intermediary accountability and procedural safeguards in India's evolving digital democracy.

Main Facts

🌟 Recent Trigger: MeitY advisories dated October 8 and 10, 2026, directed platforms to address misleading content, AI-generated deepfakes and public-order concerns.

🌟 IT Act, 2000: Section 69A empowers the government to block online information on specified grounds, including sovereignty, security and public order.

🌟 Intermediary Liability: Section 79 provides conditional safe-harbour protection to platforms hosting third-party content.

🌟 IT Rules, 2021: Rule 3(1)(d) governs removal following legally qualifying court orders or authorised-government notifications.

🌟 Accelerated Compliance: The 2026 amendments reportedly reduce the takedown compliance window from 36 hours to three hours in specified cases.

🌟 Judicial Safeguard: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) restricted intermediary takedown obligations to legally recognised actual knowledge.

Challenges

🌟 Free-Speech Erosion: Arbitrary restrictions can undermine Article 19(1)(a), subject to Article 19(2).

🌟 Executive Overreach: Broad advisories risk excessive discretionary censorship.

🌟 Algorithmic Opacity: Automated moderation may suppress legitimate political discourse.

🌟 Due-Process Deficit: Delayed appeals and inadequate explanations weaken accountability.

🌟 Digital Exclusion: Account restrictions can damage livelihoods, reputation and access to information.

Constructive Criticism

🌟 Combating misinformation is legitimate, but national security cannot become a blanket justification for censorship. Proportionality and transparency are indispensable.

Way Forward

🌟 Ensure reasoned, narrowly tailored blocking orders.

🌟 Strengthen independent oversight and judicial review.

🌟 Provide timely appeals, user notification and transparency reports.

🌟 Adopt risk-based AI-content labelling and human review.

🌟 Protect lawful criticism and journalistic expression.

Highlighted Keywords

Digital Constitutionalism, Safe Harbour, Prior Restraint, Procedural Due Process, Algorithmic Accountability.

Conclusion

A democratic state must regulate digital harm without regulating dissent; constitutional liberty must remain the cornerstone of digital governance.

CRIME, PUNISHMENT AND REFORM: JUSTICE MUST PROTECT SOCIETY AND PRESERVE HUMAN DIGNITY

When someone commits a crime, society rightly demands justice. Victims deserve protection, their suffering must be acknowledged, and offenders must be held accountable under the law.

But there is a deeper question we must also ask:

Should punishment merely make a person suffer for the past, or should the justice system also try to prevent future harm?

A responsible society needs both accountability and reform. These are not necessarily opposing goals. When applied appropriately, they can reinforce each other.

Justice must protect the public, respect victims, uphold the rule of law, and create opportunities for rehabilitation where possible.

Punishment without accountability is meaningless. But punishment without attention to preventing future crime can leave society facing the same problems again.

1. JUSTICE MUST BEGIN WITH THE VICTIM

Discussions about rehabilitation must never make victims invisible.

People affected by crime may experience physical injury, financial loss, trauma, fear, and a lasting loss of trust. Their families may also suffer consequences long after a case has ended.

A humane justice system should take their experiences seriously.

Victims need accessible legal processes, appropriate protection, timely information, and support services where available. They should not have to navigate an unnecessarily complicated system without assistance.

Restorative approaches, where legally appropriate and genuinely voluntary, may help address harm in certain cases. But victims must never be pressured to forgive an offender or participate in a process that makes them feel unsafe.

Rehabilitation must not come at the expense of victims' rights.

PUNISHMENT SHOULD BE PROPORTIONATE AND LAWFUL

Not every offence has the same consequences, circumstances, or degree of harm.

A justice system must distinguish between offences, examine evidence, consider the law, and impose appropriate consequences through fair procedures.

Serious crimes may warrant serious punishment. Public safety must remain a priority, especially where there is a continuing risk of violence or exploitation.

At the same time, punishment should not become arbitrary, discriminatory, or driven by public anger alone.

An accusation is not the same as a conviction. Every accused person deserves due process, and guilt must be determined according to law.

Justice is strongest when it is firm, fair, evidence-based, and consistent.

A RECENT WARNING FROM INDIA

On October 25, 2026, The Indian Express reported that a Bombay High Court judge highlighted the need for systematic case tracking and timely legal assistance for undertrial prisoners.

The report cited National Crime Records Bureau figures indicating that approximately 76% of India's 5.73 lakh prisoners were undertrials. It also highlighted the importance of legal awareness and effective assistance for vulnerable prisoners.

Source:
https://t.co/OTnxCdIHx3

These figures raise an important distinction: people awaiting trial are not the same as people convicted of crimes.

If cases remain unresolved for long periods, the consequences can be severe for individuals, families, and public confidence in the justice system.

Timely hearings, effective legal representation, appropriate bail decisions under the law, and better case management are therefore essential parts of fair justice.

Speed matters—but speed must never replace a fair trial.

PRISONS SHOULD PREVENT FUTURE CRIME, NOT BECOME SCHOOLS FOR IT

Imprisonment may be necessary to protect society and enforce the law. But prison conditions and management also matter.

If people leave prison with poorer mental health, no employable skills, damaged family relationships, and no lawful way to support themselves, reintegration can become difficult.

This does not mean every former prisoner will reoffend. It means that avoidable barriers to lawful living deserve serious attention.

Where appropriate, correctional institutions can provide education, vocational training, counselling, healthcare, structured work, and preparation for release.

Security remains essential. Rehabilitation does not mean ignoring misconduct or weakening prison discipline.

The objective is to ensure that people who return to society have a better opportunity to live lawfully and responsibly.

DIFFERENT OFFENDERS MAY NEED DIFFERENT RESPONSES

A young person convicted of a minor offence may need a different intervention from a repeat violent offender.

Someone whose offence is connected to substance dependence may need treatment alongside appropriate legal consequences. A person involved in organised criminal activity may require a stronger security response.

The law must determine what is permissible in each case. Decisions should be based on evidence, risk, the nature of the offence, the person's circumstances, and the rights of everyone affected.

There should be no automatic assumption that every offender can be rehabilitated in the same way—or that nobody can change.

A serious justice system recognises individual circumstances without abandoning consistent legal standards.

REHABILITATION MUST LEAD TO REAL-WORLD OPPORTUNITIES

Education and training inside prison can help, but they are not enough by themselves.

After release, people may face barriers to housing, employment, education, healthcare, and family reintegration. Some may struggle to rebuild trust. Others may return to environments associated with previous criminal activity.

Where legally appropriate, structured support can help people navigate these challenges.

Potential measures include:

Vocational training connected to actual employment opportunities.
Access to relevant healthcare and counselling.
Guidance on lawful income generation and financial management.
Family support where relationships are safe and appropriate.
Assistance accessing eligible public services.
Supervision and follow-up where required by law.

Employers and communities should not be expected to ignore the nature of an offence or any genuine safety risk. However, neither should every person who has served a sentence be treated as permanently incapable of contributing to society.

Public safety and reintegration can be pursued together through appropriate safeguards.

PREVENTION IS BETTER THAN REPEATEDLY REPAIRING THE DAMAGE

A society serious about reducing crime must also examine prevention.

Children need safe environments, education, positive role models, and protection from exploitation. Young people need lawful opportunities to develop skills and earn a livelihood.

Communities need accessible support for people facing addiction, family violence, severe distress, or other difficulties that may increase vulnerability to harmful situations.

These factors do not excuse criminal conduct, and poverty or hardship should never be treated as evidence that someone will become a criminal.

But prevention can reduce avoidable harm and help people make safer choices.

Schools, families, public institutions, businesses, and community organisations all have roles to play.

MEASURE JUSTICE BY MORE THAN THE NUMBER OF ARRESTS

A justice system needs reliable measures of performance.

Are investigations conducted lawfully? Are victims protected? Are cases progressing without avoidable delays? Can accused people access legal assistance? Are court orders implemented? Are prisons safe? Do rehabilitation programmes help eligible participants return to lawful lives?

No single statistic can answer all these questions.

Evaluation should be transparent, evidence-based, and attentive to both public safety and individual rights.

Institutions should identify failures, correct them, and remain accountable to the public.

Justice is not weakened by asking whether it works. It is strengthened by examining the evidence.

THE CONNECTION WITH GIVING AWAY SOCIETY

In my book, How to be a Social Animal — Giving Away Society: Constitution of Humanity, I explore the responsibilities that people and institutions have toward human dignity and collective well-being.

Applied to criminal justice, this raises a difficult but necessary question:

How can society hold people accountable for wrongdoing while also reducing the likelihood of future harm?

My position is that dignity should not mean impunity, and accountability should not mean abandoning every possibility of reform.

Victims deserve justice. The public deserves safety. Accused people deserve due process. Convicted offenders must face lawful consequences, and rehabilitation should be pursued where appropriate.

These principles require careful balancing, not simplistic slogans.

MY FINAL QUESTION

If a person has committed a crime, served the sentence imposed by law, and genuinely wants to rebuild their life, should society offer a lawful path toward reintegration—while maintaining appropriate safeguards and protecting victims?

And how can we make our justice system better at preventing future crimes rather than merely responding after harm has occurred?

A stronger society is not one that ignores crime. It is one that pursues justice fairly, protects people effectively, holds offenders accountable, and works to prevent tomorrow's victims.

Manish Mohan Upadhyay
Author, How to be a Social Animal — Giving Away Society: Constitution of Humanity
