WHY MORE AI AGENTS DON'T AUTOMATICALLY MEAN MORE OUTPUT

I run an autonomous engineering system. For five days it reported 25 worker minutes per accepted result as if that were the cost. It is only a lower bound. Inside the intervals where worker time was actually observed the figure is 167, and the reason is a measurement design most agent setups share.

There is a number almost everyone running AI agents quotes, and almost nobody can defend: how much work the agents are doing.

Not how many are running. Not how many tasks they closed. How much work came out the other end, got reviewed by something that was allowed to say no, and was kept.

I have been running an autonomous engineering system on my own machine for about seven weeks. It dispatches bounded coding tasks to isolated workers, each in its own git worktree, each returning an evidence receipt that an independent reviewer either accepts or blocks. The system records its own cost per accepted result on a dashboard I read every morning. For five days that dashboard said 25 worker minutes per accepted result.

When I went back through the raw data, 85 percent of those accepted results had landed in intervals where the instrument recorded no worker time at all. Restricted to the intervals where worker time was observed, the figure is 167 minutes. The two numbers are 6.6 times apart, and the reported one is the flattering one. The true system-wide cost sits somewhere at or above 25.2 and I cannot tell you where, which is the actual problem: a gauge I steered by every morning was reporting a lower bound as if it were a measurement.

The cause is not exotic. It is polling a worker count on a timer and reconstructing worker time from it. If you are running agents and watching a dashboard, there is a good chance it is built the same way, because that is the easy way to build one.

This article is the whole thing: what I measured, how, what the numbers actually support, what they do not, and a free scorecard that computes the same figures for your own setup, including the check that catches the bug.

What you will get out of it

- A definition of throughput for agent work that survives contact with a reviewer.
- The specific measurement failure that makes agent dashboards flattering, and the check that detects it.
- Real numbers from a real system, with the uncertainty stated instead of hidden.
- A decision procedure for whether to add another worker.
- A working scorecard you can run on your own data.

Chapter 0. The number everybody gets wrong

Three different things get called throughput, and they are not the same thing.

Activity is how many workers are running. It is the easiest to measure and the least useful. A worker that is running is spending money.

Completion is how many tasks reported done. Better, and still not it. An agent reporting success is a hypothesis, not a result. In my own system the self-reported success rate and the reviewed acceptance rate are different numbers, and the gap is the whole point of having a reviewer.

Accepted output is how many tasks an independent reviewer accepted. That is the only one worth optimising, because it is the only one that corresponds to something you can keep.

So the unit is: one accepted result. And the cost of it is worker time, model spend, and the human review time that came with it.

The denominator matters just as much as the numerator, and this is where it falls apart. To say "25 worker minutes per accepted result" you need two measurements from the same window: the worker time spent, and the accepted results produced. If those two are measured by different mechanisms, nothing guarantees they cover the same work. Mine did not, and I did not notice for five days.

Chapter 1. Why more workers can make you slower

Before the measurement problem, the thing being measured.

Adding a worker to an agent system is not like adding a core to a CPU. Every extra worker adds load to shared stages that do not scale with it:

Context acquisition. Each worker has to learn the part of the codebase it is about to touch. That cost is paid per worker, not once. Two workers on adjacent files pay it twice and often learn contradictory things.

Collision and ownership. Two workers that touch the same file produce a merge problem that did not exist before. The fix is one writer per surface, which means that past a certain point extra workers have nothing uncontested left to do.

Review. This is the one that bites. Review capacity is close to fixed, because a reviewer that scales with the workers is just more unreviewed work wearing a hat. Eight workers feeding one review stage do not produce eight times the accepted output. They produce a queue.

Integration. Accepted work still has to land. Branches diverge while they wait. The longer the queue, the more likely a branch needs rework before it can merge, which sends it back to a worker and starts the cycle again.

Abandonment. Work that is never reviewed, never merged, or superseded before it lands is pure cost. In my own repository there are branches sitting at double digit dirty-file counts that will never be merged. Every minute in them was paid for.

The shape of this is a queueing system with a narrow stage in the middle, and the classic property of such systems is that the bottleneck does not move when you add capacity upstream. It gets worse, because the queue in front of it lengthens.

That is a well understood argument and I am not claiming to have discovered it. What I can add is a measurement, and an account of how hard it is to measure honestly.

Chapter 2. Inside the system, in public-safe terms

Enough of the architecture to make the numbers meaningful.

A scheduler fires on a timer. On each tick it reads the current state, decides how many bounded tasks to dispatch, and launches each one as an isolated worker with its own git worktree and its own acceptance contract. A task has a budget and a stop rule written into its brief. When a worker finishes, it writes an evidence receipt: what it changed, what tests it ran, what the output was.

A separate reviewer reads the receipt and the diff and writes a verdict file. The verdict is ACCEPTED or it is not, and a non-acceptance has to carry a demonstrated failure, not an opinion. That rule exists because reviewers that block on taste produce infinite loops.

Accepted work merges. The verdict files stay on disk as the permanent record. That record is the dataset in this article: a directory of verdict files with timestamps, and a scheduler log with one line per tick.

Two numbers from the scheduler log matter for what follows, and both are printed on every single line of it:

- The worker count at that moment.
- The task timeout: 1100 seconds, which is 18.3 minutes. No worker can live longer than that.

Chapter 3. The measurement, and the bug inside it

The window: 2026-10-17 07:47 to 2026-10-22 04:48, local time. 342 scheduler ticks. 89 verdict files written inside the window: 66 accepted, 23 not accepted. Acceptance rate 0.74.

Worker time is not logged directly. It is reconstructed, which is where the trouble starts. Each tick records the worker count at that instant. The estimate treats that count as constant until the next tick, multiplies by the gap, and sums. Over the window that gives 1,666 worker minutes. Divide by 66 accepted results and you get 25.2 worker minutes per accepted result. That is the number the dashboard reported, and the number I believed.

Now the part I missed. The scheduler ticks every 20 minutes. I checked the gaps between all 342 ticks: the median is 20.0 minutes, the shortest is 16.7. And the maximum worker lifetime, printed on every line of the same log, is 18.3 minutes.

The sampler is slower than the thing it is sampling.

A worker that starts after one tick and finishes before the next is never seen. The interval is recorded as zero workers, and every minute that worker spent is counted as zero. Recorded as zero and did not run look identical in the data.

Be careful about how strong a claim that is. 18.3 minutes is the maximum worker lifetime, not the minimum, so a 20 minute interval makes a complete miss possible; it does not prove that every short worker was missed, and some workers clearly were seen. The reverse is also worth stating plainly, because it is the trap I nearly wrote into this article: no fixed polling interval guarantees you see everything. Halving the interval to 9.2 minutes would bound misses for workers that last longer than the interval and would do nothing at all for a worker that lives 90 seconds. Polling faster narrows the hole. Only per-worker start and end events close it.

So I went back and asked a question I should have asked first: for each accepted result, what was the recorded worker count in the interval it landed in?

Concurrent workers recorded / Wall hours / Worker minutes / Accepted / Not accepted / Worker min per accepted
|---|---|---|---|---|---
0 / 89.5 / 0 / 56 / 19 / undefined
1 / 20.2 / 1,212 / 9 / 4 / 134.7
2 / 3.3 / 393 / 1 / 0 / 392.7
3 / 0.3 / 61 / 0 / 0 / undefined
All / 113.3 / 1,666 / 66 / 23 / 25.2

Fifty six of the sixty six accepted results, 85 percent of them, landed in intervals where the instrument recorded zero workers. Those results have no measured cost at all. They were divided into a pile of worker minutes they had nothing to do with.

All 1,666 measured worker minutes sit in the non-zero rows by definition, and those rows contain 10 accepted results. Restricted to the intervals where worker time was observed, the figure is 1,666 divided by 10, or 166.6 worker minutes per accepted result. The two numbers are 6.6 times apart.

Be precise about what each of those numbers is, because this is exactly where it is easy to cheat.

25.2 is a lower bound, not an estimate. Every accepted result is counted in the denominator, but the numerator is an undercount of worker time, since unobserved workers contribute zero. True worker minutes are at least 1,666, so the true cost per accepted result is at least 25.2 and could be anything above it.

166.6 is a conditional figure, not the true cost. It is the cost per accepted result within the intervals where worker time was observed, and those intervals were selected by the instrument rather than at random. It rests on 10 accepted results.

The true system-wide figure is unknown. Attribution coverage of 0.152 is not a correction factor; it is a statement that 85 percent of the output cannot be tied to any measured cost. No arithmetic on this dataset recovers the real number. What the dataset does support, firmly, is that the reported figure was a floor presented as a measurement, and the gap between it and the attributable figure is a factor of 6.6.

Why so many zero-worker intervals? Two reasons, and I can only partly separate them. Some is the aliasing above: short workers born and dead inside one 20 minute gap. Some is lag: a verdict file is written when the review is written, which can be well after the work. Both push accepted results into intervals where no worker time was recorded, and both are properties of the instrument rather than the system being measured. That is the uncomfortable part. The instrument was wrong in a way that made the system look better.

What about 1 worker versus 2?

The table hints at the thing the article is named after: 134.7 worker minutes per accepted at one worker, 392.7 at two. Nearly three times worse.

I am not going to tell you that is a result. It rests on 9 accepted results in one bucket and 1 in the other. The worker count was chosen by a governor reacting to machine load, so the two-worker periods are the busier, more contended periods by construction. Task difficulty was not held constant. Any of those could produce this on its own.

What it is: a directionally consistent observation, too small to carry weight, in a system where the mechanism that would cause it is already known to exist. The right response is not to publish it as a finding. It is to run the controlled version, which I will, and which the scorecard below is built to record.

If you came here for "15 agents are slower than 3, here is the graph", I do not have that graph and neither does anyone else I have been able to find. What I have is the measurement framework, one real dataset with its flaws exposed, and the specific instrument bug that makes most such graphs untrustworthy.

Chapter 4. Where the bottleneck actually sits

Strip the measurement problem away and look at the shape of the window.

113.3 wall hours. Workers recorded as running for 20.2 hours of it at one worker, 3.3 at two, 0.3 at three. For roughly 79 percent of the wall clock the system recorded no workers at all, and yet most of the accepted work shows up in those stretches.

Even allowing generously for unobserved workers, the picture is of a system that is not worker-bound. It is bound by what happens between dispatches: deciding what to dispatch, reviewing what came back, and merging it. Adding workers to that system buys very little, and the thing it does buy most reliably is a longer review queue.

This is the practical reason the "add more agents" instinct disappoints. High worker utilisation is not a goal. It is only good if accepted output per worker hour holds up as you add them. When the constrained stage is review or integration, the sign of improvement is not busier workers. It is the queue in front of review getting shorter.

Chapter 5. The governor, as a design pattern

If a worker is not the unit of capacity, something has to decide when work is dispatched at all. In my system that is a governor, and I am describing it here as a pattern rather than claiming a verified product.

The governor holds a small number of rules:

- Objective fidelity. A task that does not serve the current objective does not get dispatched, however good it looks. Found-it-so-build-it is how a week disappears.
- Previously accepted evidence. If a question was already answered and the answer was accepted, it is not re-opened without a demonstrated reason.
- Bounded exploration. Every task has a budget and a stop rule. Over budget is a blocked result, not a slow green one.
- Action risk classes. Reversible and in scope runs without asking. Spending money, sending something outward, or anything irreversible stops and asks a human.
- Stop and escalate. Conflict between owners, a failed safety floor, or a missing permission stops mutation and preserves state.

The honest status line: these are implemented and in use. They are not independently verified as a product, and this article is not a release announcement for them. The reason they are relevant here is that every one of them reduces the number of workers you need, which is a cheaper lever than adding workers.

Chapter 6. The scorecard you can use

The companion artifact is a single page with no dependencies, no network calls, no analytics and no storage. You can download two files and open it from your filesystem. Nothing you type leaves the page.

It does three jobs.

One: it checks your instrument before it computes anything. Enter your sampler period and the shortest worker lifetime you care about observing. It tells you whether a worker can slip between two samples, and it refuses to describe any polling interval as a guarantee. With my real numbers, a 20 minute interval and an 18.3 minute maximum lifetime, it returns:

CAN MISS WORKERS. A worker shorter than the 20 min interval can start and finish unseen. Sampling every 9.2 min would bound misses for workers longer than that interval, and still not for shorter ones. Per-worker start and end events are the only reliable fix.

Two: it scores a measurement window. Attempted, accepted, rejected, wall hours, worker hours, review hours, model cost. It returns acceptance ratio, accepted per worker hour, worker minutes per accepted, cost per accepted, integration ratio and rework share.

It also has a field most dashboards do not: accepted results that fall inside observed worker time. The ratio of that to total accepted is the attribution coverage. At coverage 1 your cost figure is sound. My window scores 0.152, and the tool flags attribution as broken, shows both figures side by side, 25.2 across all accepted results and 166.6 within observed intervals, and labels the first a lower bound rather than a result. It does not pretend the gap is a correction factor. That contrast is the single most useful thing the tool does.

Three: it compares two windows and gives a verdict. Load the measured one-worker and two-worker windows and it returns:

SCALING HURT. Accepted per worker hour 0.446 to 0.153. Change: minus 65.7 percent.

with a line underneath reminding you that a difference between two windows is not a controlled result.

Two deliberate choices in the code. Every ratio with an empty denominator returns null, never zero and never infinity, because a missing measurement and a measured zero are different facts and conflating them is how you end up with a confident wrong number. And a measured zero is a verdict: a window that produced nothing in an observed hour of worker time has told you something real.

The whole calculation core is 145 lines, 94 of them code, with 18 tests covering division by zero, missing fields, negative inputs, accepted exceeding attempted, worker hours exceeding workers times wall hours, unit conversion, the sampling-interval boundary cases and extreme values. The tests run with node --test. One of them caught a real mistake I had made in the comparison logic, where I had treated a measured zero as an absence. That is the same category of error as the one this entire article is about, which I think is the honest note to end the engineering on.

Chapter 7. How to apply this on Monday

In order, because the order matters.

1. Check whether a worker can slip between two of your samples. Compare your polling interval with the shortest worker you care about. If a worker can start and finish inside one interval, your worker time is an undercount and your cost per accepted result is a floor, not a measurement. Polling faster shrinks the hole for longer workers and never closes it for short ones.

2. Define accepted before you measure anything. Something independent of the worker has to be allowed to say no, and a rejection has to carry a demonstrated reason rather than a preference. Without that, throughput is just activity with better branding.

3. Measure worker time, do not reconstruct it. This is the real fix and it is not a faster sampler. Have each worker record its own start and end. Worker hours then become a sum of measured intervals, attribution coverage goes to 1 by construction, and the polling question disappears instead of getting smaller. I am moving to that; a faster tick is only a stopgap that reduces the hole for long workers.

4. Find the constrained stage before adding capacity. If review and integration are waiting on work, more workers help. If work is waiting on review, more workers make it worse. You can usually tell by looking at how long something sits between accepted and merged.

5. Spend on routing before spending on workers. Better task boundaries, one writer per surface, and a clear acceptance contract raise accepted output per worker hour without adding a single worker.

6. Add one worker, then measure the same window again. Not two. If accepted per worker hour falls, you have your answer, and it cost you one experiment.

The limits of all of this

The things I would attack if I were reading this.

- One system, one operator, five days. Not a benchmark. My workloads are not yours.
- The 166.6 figure rests on 10 accepted results, in intervals the instrument selected rather than a random sample. It is a conditional figure, not a replacement true value.
- The true system-wide cost per accepted result is unknown. 25.2 is a lower bound. Nothing in this dataset identifies the real number, and I am not going to pretend otherwise.
- The one versus two worker comparison is observational and tiny. Treat it as a hypothesis with a mechanism, nothing more.
- Verdict timestamps lag the work, so some of the zero-worker mass is lag rather than missed workers. This dataset cannot separate the two. Recording work start and end directly fixes both at once, and I have not done it yet.
- The acceptance standard is mine. A stricter reviewer would lower every acceptance ratio here. Throughput measured against a weak reviewer is a vanity number, and no tool can detect that for you.
- No controlled experiment yet. The protocol is: fixed task family, fixed model route, fixed reviewer, randomised worker count, at least 30 accepted results per arm. That is the next issue.

The right question

"How many agents can I run" is a question about your budget. It has an easy, expensive answer.

The question that pays is: what gets accepted, how fast, at what total cost, and with how much of my attention? Every one of those has a denominator, and a denominator you cannot defend is not a measurement.

The reason I am opening with my own broken gauge rather than a clean result is that the broken gauge is the more useful finding. Anyone can produce a chart with agent counts on one axis. Almost nobody shows you whether their instrument could see what it was counting, or whether the number on the dashboard is a measurement or a floor. Mine was a floor for five days while I read it every morning.

Check yours. The scorecard will tell you in about a minute, and if your answer is the same as mine, the fix is to stop polling and start recording.

The scorecard is free and runs entirely in your browser. No signup, no network calls, no analytics, nothing stored.

https://t.co/nsE6rnodLM

let's say 𝘊𝘭𝘢𝘶𝘥𝘦 𝘊𝘰𝘥𝘦 created 𝘺𝘰𝘶𝘳 𝘤𝘩𝘦𝘤𝘬𝘰𝘶t page, 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘯 𝘸𝘳𝘰𝘵𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘵𝘦𝘴𝘵𝘴 𝘧𝘰𝘳 𝘪𝘵𝘴 𝘰𝘸𝘯 𝘤𝘰𝘥𝘦, ran them, and they all pass!

think about it! a test is just code that checks other code, and here the same session wrote both. 

so if it guessed wrong in the code, it guessed wrong in the tests too, and green only means 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗱𝗲 𝗮𝗴𝗿𝗲𝗲𝘀 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗶𝘁𝘀𝗲𝗹𝗳!

so when you tested it, you saw "12" tests and "12" green checks, and you tested and paid with your own card, and everything worked!

now Claude keeps building all week, and it adds 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘁𝘀 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝗱𝗮𝘆:

"12 𝘵𝘦𝘴𝘵𝘴 𝘰𝘯 𝘔𝘰𝘯𝘥𝘢𝘺... 40 𝘣𝘺 𝘞𝘦𝘥𝘯𝘦𝘴𝘥𝘢𝘺... 120 𝘣𝘺 𝘍𝘳𝘪𝘥𝘢𝘺, 𝘢𝘭𝘭 𝘨𝘳𝘦𝘦𝘯"

that's 𝟭𝟮𝟬 𝗴𝗿𝗲𝗲𝗻 𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘁𝘀, and not one of them tries a declined card: Claude assumed every card goes through, so the code and the tests both skip it. more tests won't save you, each new one copies the same guess. 

meanwhile, a customer whose card was declined just got their order for free!! 

𝘀𝗼 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁?

let's learn about "𝙩𝙚𝙨𝙩𝙨 𝙛𝙧𝙤𝙢 𝙩𝙝𝙚 𝙨𝙥𝙚𝙘"

the idea is simple:

write down what the checkout must do before the code exists (that's the spec), and let the tests come from that list, not from the code.

• the spec: a few plain lines, like "a declined card makes no order" and "an order over $50 ships free"
• the tests: a fresh session that never saw the code turns each line into a test
• the check: run the tests against the code. a red test means the code or the spec is wrong, and you decide which

tests come in three layers
- small to big: unit (one function, like the free shipping math)
- integration (the pieces together: your database, the payment service)
- end-to-end (a real click through checkout). use the smallest layer that proves the line.

careful: "all tests pass" isn't "the product works". a case nobody wrote down never gets tested, so read the spec yourself before Claude builds: it's the one part only you can get right.

ask Claude:
"write a short spec for my checkout as plain lines of what must happen and show it to me first, then have a separate sub-agent write unit, integration and end-to-end tests from that spec only, without reading how you built it, run them, and tell me which lines fail."

you don't have to write this code yourself. you just have to know 𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘁𝘀 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝗽𝗲𝗰 exists, 𝘀𝗼 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗮𝘀𝗸 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗶𝘁 𝗯𝗲𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝘀𝗵𝗶𝗽.

Use these portable rules directly for your codebase.

Portable agent rules — tests, code shape, design slop
Project-agnostic. Copy the three sections below into any repo's AGENTS.md (or CLAUDE.md, .cursorrules, CONTRIBUTING.md) and delete the framing. Nothing here names a product, a file or a dependency.

Numbers marked (tune) are defaults chosen to be uncomfortable enough to matter; adjust per project but keep them explicit.

1. Tests must prove something
A test is a claim about behaviour that could break, and whose breaking would be silent or expensive. Anything else is maintenance cost with no return.

Write the test when it pins:

A rule that came from measured or documented platform behaviour — the API that returns 401 for a missing permission, the record that arrives as 400 instead of 404, the date field that is epoch millis on one endpoint and ISO on another. These are exactly the facts a future refactor will "clean up" wrongly.
A boundary where the wrong answer is invisible: an empty result set, a cursor the API silently ignored, an empty response body, a timeout that returned partial data.
An invariant a future change could break without noticing: a write is never retried; two duplicated config blocks stay identical; a pure module never imports the platform.
Arithmetic whose error is subtle: contrast ratios, attempt counts, backoff steps, page arithmetic, currency rounding.
Do not write the test when it only:

Restates the body of the function under test.
Covers a trivial getter, setter or formatter with no branching.
Asserts a constant equals its own literal — unless other code depends on that literal, in which case it is a contract, not a constant.
Exercises framework, browser or vendor behaviour you do not control.
Repeats a path a behavioural test two lines up already covers, with no distinct failure mode.
The check: finish the sentence "this fails if …" with something a user would notice or a reviewer would miss. If you cannot, delete the test.

Two corollaries:

Prove a new gate fails before trusting it. Plant the violation, watch it fail with a readable message, remove it. A check never seen red is indistinguishable from one that cannot go red.
Test count is an outcome, never a target. One sharp test beats eleven shallow ones; the shallow ones make the real ones slower to run and harder to find.
2. Design pass before every commit
Walk the diff against these nine. A tripped item is fixed now, or deliberately accepted and recorded in the decisions log with the reason.

FactorWhat it looks likeThe fix
Implicit couplingA module keyed by a string another module must reproduce exactly (endpoint labels, storage keys, event names, message shapes). The two drift apart and nothing fails.Give the shared thing one exported identity and have callers reference it, never retype it. Validate at the boundary so a mismatch is loud.
Layer-first folderslib/ accumulating one flat pile of unrelated files because "that is where helpers go".Fine while small. Past ~5–7 files, group feature-first (lib/export/, lib/render/) instead of growing a utils.js.
DuplicationThe same rule stated twice — two limit ranges, two copies of a config block, one fact stored in two https://t.co/4ZZAgA54vF constant, one function, one owner. Where duplication is physically forced (JSON config, CSS media query), add a test asserting the copies are equal.
Representable illegal statesA result object where status: 200 with kind: 'error' is constructible; flags that can disagree with the data they describe.Derive one field from another instead of storing both. Make the shape per-variant: each error kind carries only the fields it needs.
God filesAny file approaching ~400 lines (tune), or a file with more than one reason to change.Split along the seam that already exists, before it becomes urgent. A test can hold the line so it fails instead of drifting.
Shotgun surgeryOne conceptual change touching many files — "add an endpoint" edits five places.Introduce the missing registry or seam so the change has one home.
Layering violationsA pure layer importing the platform (chrome.*, window, fs), a renderer calling the network, UI reading credentials. Mocked platforms hide this, so behavioural tests still https://t.co/PcbpZMoj1k layer owns the platform and the network; everything below takes injected dependencies. Add a source-level check, because mocks make this invisible at runtime.
Pass-through wrappersA function that forwards arguments to another and adds no policy.Delete it, or give it a reason to exist: timeout, retry, logging, normalising, validation.
Errors / validation not at the boundaryNull checks scattered through renderers; the same payload shape guessed in three places; raw vendor objects flowing inward.Validate and normalise once, at ingest: external response → internal shape at the API boundary, user input → typed value at the UI boundary. A renderer checking for undefined is evidence the boundary did not do its job.
3. Design slop indicators
The marks of generated filler. Any one makes a purpose-built tool look like a template; several together make it look dishonest about how much thought went into it. Check the diff against this list in the same pass as section 2.

IndicatorWhy it reads as generatedWhat to do instead
TagsA pill or badge on every field — category, count, host, source, type — so the row becomes a row of chips. Decoration standing in for hierarchy: if everything is tagged, nothing is prioritised.Plain text for labels and values. A pill only for state that changes and that the user acts on (running, complete, failed). Never two pills for one fact.
Italicised wordsItalics as the emphasis of last resort, sprinkled through labels and helper text to make flat copy feel designed.Weight and colour carry emphasis. Italic is reserved for quoted user content — that is data, not styling.
Display serif + negative kerningThe strongest single tell: an editorial display serif (Instrument Serif, Playfair, Fraunces) imported into a data utility, with tracking crushed to −0.03em or tighter to imitate print polish. It trades legibility for a mood the product has not https://t.co/YvvbjKoWrw bundled, legible typeface. Heading tracking no tighter than −0.01em, body at 0.
Over the top detailed UIShowing every computable number because it can: nine statistics, four progress readouts, a log tail. A utility is judged on the one task it exists for.The primary surface shows state, one count, the destination, one action. Detail belongs in the report, not the surface used while working.
DividersA hairline between every row and section until the surface reads as a ruled spreadsheet.Spacing separates. A border appears only where a region genuinely ends or a card needs an edge.
Multiple colour shades and opacitiesFive blues, three greys per surface, stray rgba() in components, tinted backgrounds that encode nothing. A palette that cannot be named is not doing work.Status colour means exactly one thing. Everything else is a token. Opacity is for disabled state only. A genuinely new shade becomes a token before it becomes a value.
Containers with bordersEvery group wrapped in a bordered box, then those boxes nested inside another. Boxes used as layout, hiding a spacing problem behind a https://t.co/fCj1nJpq0O card where a group is genuinely a unit. Nesting is usually a layout problem wearing a box.
DiagramsA diagram in the product UI: boxes and arrows describing the pipeline, the more detailed the worse. They date instantly, contradict the code within a release, and cannot be read at a glance.If the flow cannot be told in one sentence plus a progress bar, the flow is the problem. Diagrams belong in docs — hand-drawn if anywhere — not in the product.
Section numbering"01 — Setup", "02 — Connect": numbers nobody will cite, implying a procedure where there is only a page.Numbered steps only when the order is mandatory, and then they are steps, not sections.
A dense interface can look busy — that is data, and it is welcome. Busy from styling is not the same thing.

Wiring it up
Put sections 1–3 above your project-specific rules, or below them if the project has binding design authority. If a project has a design doc that governs tokens and values, state explicitly that the design doc wins on values and any conflict is raised, not decided.
Keep a docs/decisions.md (numbered, dated, append-only, superseded rather than edited) and a docs/learning.md (rule-shaped lessons: what bit you and the rule it produced). A rule that lives only in a chat transcript is lost.
Update the docs in the same commit as the code they describe. A stale doc is a defect.
Record deviations instead of breaking the rules silently — a rule without an escape hatch gets ignored wholesale.
One-paragraph version
For small repos where a single page is enough:

Write a test only when it pins measured platform behaviour, an invisible boundary, an invariant a future change could break silently, or arithmetic whose error is subtle — and be able to finish "this fails if …" with something a user would notice. Never test that a function returns its own body. Before each commit, check the diff for implicit coupling (a string two modules must retype), god files, duplication, representable illegal states, layering violations, and validation that happens below the boundary. Check the UI for the marks of generated filler: a pill on every field, decorative italics, a display serif with crushed tracking, every number shown because it can be, hairlines between every row, a palette of unnamed shades and opacities, nested bordered boxes, diagrams in the product, and 01/02 section numbering. A dense interface may be busy from data; busy from styling is not the same thing.

The post (from October 29, 2026) says police were “chased out of London last night by hordes of Muslims,” with one officer hospitalized, and criticizes the lack of response from Keir Starmer and Sadiq Khan. The attached video is real footage, but it is old and misrepresented.
It shows the disorder on Edgware Road (Paddington area) on the night of July 9–10, 2026, after France beat Morocco 2-0 in the World Cup quarterfinals. Moroccan fans (many in team shirts or with the Moroccan flag) blocked the road, threw bottles and set off fireworks/pyrotechnics. One officer was hit in the head by a glass bottle and taken to hospital (he was later discharged); four people were arrested for violent disorder. Police deployed extra officers (including in public-order gear), remained on scene, dispersed the group, and reopened the road around 1 a.m. Contemporary reporting from the BBC, Guardian, and others describes it as football-related disorder, not a religious or political “hordes of Muslims” attack that drove police from the city.
Fact-checks (including from Portuguese outlets covering the same viral clip) have previously labeled versions of this narrative false for exactly these reasons: the video is authentic but the accompanying claims of police fleeing a Muslim mob and of religious motivation are not supported by the evidence. There are no credible reports of any comparable event “last night” (around October 28–29, 2026).
In short: old World Cup fan disorder, not a recent Islamist chase of police out of London.

Have you seen a chart like this & wondered if it accurately represents current COVID-19 prevalence?

It doesn't.

The account creating these charts (Mike Hoerger) is a psychologist with zero expertise in infectious disease epidemiology.

His methods are not peer-reviewed.

Checked against raw data his claims don’t hold up.

Professor Michael Fuhrer (@MichaelSFuhrer) just published a deep-dive that exposes major flaws in these charts!

Main points:

👉  Every single number is based on CDC's wastewater viral activity level (WVAL).  The global scientific consensus is that this can't be done.

A 2024 report by the combined National Academies of Sciences, Engineering & Medicine found that the science is not there yet to accomplish this.

👉  The WVAL is a relative measure & does not measure any quantity. 

"This is a fundamental category error & makes the methodology impossible.

The WVAL is not an absolute measure of any quantity, instead it is a z-score measured relative to a baseline of the two most recent years, with baselines updated every six months. 

Hence it cannot, even in principle, be used to estimate prevalence of Covid-19, or be compared across years to estimate how prevalence has changed in time."

👉  All of the numbers on the PMC Dashboard are derived from unscientific prevalence estimates.

"The estimates of excess deaths resulting from new daily/weekly infections as displayed on the PMC Dashboard are in fact adjusted to match an actuarial prediction made in 2024. 

These estimates therefore do not add any information beyond what was predicted (not observed) in 2024, and the 2024 report appears to be out of date and inconsistent with more recent actuarial analysis."

In summary Mike Hoerger uses this method to estimate numbers of new infections down to the county level in the US but his entire methodology is flawed & these charts don't (and technically can't) represent reality.

If you see this chart call it out for what it is: 

Misinformation.

Here is @michael_hoerger referencing the "swiss excess deaths" report.

This is one of the more deceptive claims I've ever seen.

Hoerger takes a cherry-picked reading of a Swiss actuarial prediction from 2024, which estimated U.S. excess mortality at 3–7% in 2023 & projected a gradual decline. 

It's almost 2027. 

A 2024 report using 2023 data is no longer valid.
https://t.co/UvimngK7c4

He deceptively interprets the high end of that 2023 range for 2025 and keeps applying elevated figures into later years, effectively freezing the 2023 upper bound rather than following the report’s own downward trajectory. 

He continues using similar high numbers for 2026 even though the modeled path shows excess continuing to fall. 

Most importantly, he ignores more recent RGA actuarial work showing U.S. excess returning to pre-pandemic expectations!
https://t.co/7rhfHWS6Pq

And he also ignores the official data post 2023 that shows:

A) The USA hasn't had measurable excess since 2022.

B) Age-standardized mortality rates in the USA has been NEGATIVE since 2024

C) US life expectancy marked a record high in 2024

D) The US death rate dropped to a record low in 2025

You can search his timeline all day but you'll never see him referencing this actual data (outside of denying it.)

And anyone who challenges his false claims?

They get blocked.

A simple "I accept" checkbox won't save you under the DPDP Act. 

Most platforms treat consent like a formality, but DPDP changes the rules:

- Purpose Limitation: Blanket consent is out. Purpose must be specific and explicit.
- Defined Timelines: No indefinite data holding. You must state the exact duration.
- Right to Withdraw & Erase: If a user withdraws consent or asks for data erasure, processing must stop, and data must be purged immediately.

A basic cookie banner is only 1% of compliance. Real consent management requires full lifecycle governance.

The Schedule to the DPDP Act has six specific penalty ceilings and one catch-all. Entry 7 sets a penalty of up to 50 crore rupees for breaching any provision of the Act or the Rules that does not have its own entry.

I would not ignore this entry, because it covers many everyday duties: giving a notice under section 5, getting valid consent under section 6, erasing data under section 8(7) and running a grievance mechanism under section 8(10). The Centre has issued a notice to messaging platform Telegram, directing it to take concrete measures within 15 days to curb the widespread circulation of pirated films, OTT content and other copyrighted audio-visual material on its platform.

The notice, issued by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting (I&B) on July 4, asks Telegram to strengthen its mechanisms for detecting, reporting, disabling access to and removing infringing content. The move is aimed at safeguarding India's creator economy, film industry, broadcasters, OTT platforms, producers and distributors.

The government has also instructed the platform to take action against repeat offenders, including channels, groups, bots, accounts, administrators and associated entities involved in the dissemination of pirated content.

In addition, Telegram has been asked to furnish details of its grievance redressal mechanism available to producers, OTT platforms and law-enforcement agencies, and to submit an Action Taken Report within 15 days outlining the measures implemented to prevent and remove piracy-related material.

The notice signals a shift towards greater platform accountability rather than relying solely on individual takedown requests. The government has previously acted against more than 3,000 Telegram channels allegedly carrying pirated content.

The development comes amid increasing scrutiny of digital platforms over content regulation and compliance. Telegram was also temporarily blocked in India until June 22 in connection with concerns surrounding the NEET-UG re-examination process following allegations of a paper leak and a subsequent investigation by the Central Bureau of Investigation.

And this is precisely why the situation is so dangerous.

The 2025 Nobel Prize in Economics recognised research explaining how innovation and "creative destruction" challenge established economic structures. New entrants threaten incumbents by introducing new ideas, technologies and competition.

The same principle has a powerful democratic parallel.

New journalists challenge established media monopolies. Independent creators challenge controlled narratives. Citizen journalists challenge institutional gatekeeping.

When emerging voices are disproportionately silenced, the result is not merely content moderation. It risks protecting the existing information monopoly from democratic competition.

A government does not need to shut down every newspaper or arrest every journalist to suppress dissent. If independent voices can be systematically restricted before they become influential, the next generation of critical journalism can be strangled at birth.

This is how digital authoritarianism can operate without formally declaring censorship.

And the biggest concern goes far beyond digital sovereignty.

A foreign private corporation controlling the visibility, distribution and survival of political speech has enormous potential influence over public opinion.

If political criticism is disproportionately suppressed while favourable narratives remain amplified, electoral competition itself can be distorted.

Manipulation of political visibility can become manipulation of electoral choices. And interference with free and fair elections is an attack on the sovereignty of the Indian people themselves.

The Constitution derives its authority from "We, the People", not from Meta's algorithms, corporate executives or any ruling political party.

Yet where does an ordinary citizen seek justice when platform appeals are ineffective and even the independence and accountability of institutions such as the Election Commission and judiciary are being publicly questioned?  1/2

Mandarins and moguls muzzle dissent

by Prabhu Chawla 

That right to receive, which Indian courts read into Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution, is being hollowed out by two hands in sinister concert—the babu wielding a blocking order and the digital billionaire wielding an algorithm.

Every tyranny begins with a fight over who may speak. Every freedom expires when a coterie of the powerful decides who may listen. Speech is a covenant between the one who utters and the one who hears, and a society is only as free as the ear of its humblest citizen.

The village chaupal, the smoky coffee house and the querulous letters page were imperfect parliaments of the people, raucous and often mistaken; yet, owned by nobody. That popular platform has now been fenced and privatised. People believe that they conversing with one another, but actually they are murmuring through machines that belong to someone else.

Button-driven machines decide in tenebrous silence whose words shall travel and whose shall perish unheard. John Milton pleaded for “the liberty to know, to utter, and to argue freely according to conscience, above all liberties”. The sequencing of his verbs was symbolic. Knowing came first. A citizen denied unfiltered information cannot fashion an honest opinion, and a citizen bereft of honest opinion is not a voter but a vessel. That right to receive, which Indian courts read into Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution, is being hollowed out by two hands in sinister concert—the babu wielding a blocking order and the digital billionaire wielding an algorithm.

The latest confession came from the algorithm itself. Last weekend, X began showing users which of their posts carried a reach-limiting label. One circulating screenshot shows a creator with 229 posts in September, two of them branded as spam by an automated sentinel and hidden from everyone who did not already follow the account. No human scrutiny was done on them and no appeal preceded the punishment. It is like the jailor handing the prisoner a receipt for his own confinement.

When Elon Musk bought Twitter in 2022 he declared, “By free speech, I simply mean that which matches the law.” In India, the law has proved wonderfully elastic. In the first half of 2025, X received 29,118 demands to remove content and obeyed 26,641 of them, a compliance rate of 91.49 percent. The self-anointed absolutist became an obsequious subordinate.

The apparatus feeding that invisible hand has since grown Brobdingnagian. Between March and July 2026, central and state agencies sent nearly 1.95 lakh blocking orders to Instagram, Facebook and YouTube—about 1,275 a day or one every 68 seconds. Most of these missives travelled through Sahyog, which lets ministries and police forces order takedowns while bypassing the safeguards of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act. Meta has wired itself into it, so flagged content can vanish unseen by any human being.

The surge coincided with the student agitation over examination scandals, which ended only when the education minister resigned. In October, protesters demanding the removal of the Chief Election Commissioner converged on Jantar Mantar. Delhi Police issued at least 200 takedown orders in days, five times their weekly norm. Among them were footage of Rahul Gandhi’s press conference and a reel of a protester holding nothing but a blank placard. The Cockroach Janta Party has seen its accounts withheld, suspended and restored by turns.

The Karnataka High Court has ruled that a foreign company cannot invoke Article 19. The Supreme Court has frozen every challenge pending in high courts. Nor is the opposition unblemished. Congress-ruled Karnataka drafted a law prescribing up to seven years in prison and fines of Rs 10 lakh for “fake news”. Power is promiscuous, and whoever clutches it covets a mute button.

Behind the servile civil servants now stand the billionaires. Musk owns X and Grok. Mark Zuckerberg presides over Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp and Threads. Sunder Pichai runs Alphabet for Larry Page and Sergey Brin, while Neal Mohan’s YouTube decides what half a billion Indians watch next. Jeff Bezos owns Amazon and The Washington Post, Zhang Yiming built TikTok and Pavel Durov governs Telegram. Their convictions pirouette with the political weather. Zuckerberg scrapped professional fact-checking after the 2024 American election and admitted the result had partly prompted it. Bezos confined his newspaper’s opinion pages to two approved pillars and told dissenters to publish elsewhere. Donald Trump, exiled from Twitter, simply built his own platform. These men do not convey the conversation. They curate it, bending with vulpine instinct toward whoever holds the licence or the regulator’s pen.

The result is an inversion in the very direction of information. Social media was born as a convivial conversation among equals and is expiring as a monologue. The ‘For You’ feed serves advertisers, regulators and the proprietor’s politics, while the citizen is demoted from interlocutor to supine recipient. One may still speak. But that one simply cannot be found.

A rival perception fervently held in nationalist circles insists that the algorithm is a covert partisan that lavishes massive traction upon strident left-wing voices bent on regime change through incitement. Its supporters cite the youthful violent protests that unseated leaders in Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Nepal. To them, every viral hashtag is a latent Molotov cocktail and every Gen Z influencer a foot soldier of some foreign-financed insurrection.

The fear is not wholly imaginary because algorithms reward fury, and fury is the currency of revolt. The machine has no ideology except engagement. That is precisely why the perception is aptly suitable power to seek a deterrent. If a government is convinced that the algorithm is plotting its overthrow then it weaponises its self to silence every critic. The spectre of regime change becomes the pretext for the regime’s survival.

The hypocrisy turns grotesque when one asks what these panoptic systems fail to see. In 2025, America’s child-protection clearinghouse received more than 21 million reports of suspected child sexual exploitation, nearly 11 million from Meta alone. In January 2026, Grok was generating sexualised images of women and minors on demand, until Indonesia and Malaysia blocked it. These algorithms are ferocious toward dialogue and flaccid toward depravity. None of this denies that the platforms are biased and polluted.

But its cure must be lawful, open and proportionate. Every blocking order should be published with reasons and every affected citizen heard by an independent agency before the axe falls. Sahyog should be dismantled, and Indians deserve a statutory right to algorithmic transparency, a chronological feed and platforms judged by the abuse they prevent rather than the reports they file.

A democratic country does not perish when its newspapers close. It perishes when its people stop noticing what they are no longer permitted to see. If babus and billionaires complete this sterilised world, the next generation will inherit a nation fluent in opinion and famished for facts. And when the silence is complete, there will be no platform left to protest or project.

elon musk's grok bot found a hidden profile on my phone that recorded my screen, camera and location for 19 days. $12,400 was stolen from my bank account using 2FA codes screenshotted off my screen in real time. all from 20 minutes of charging at the airport

my flight was delayed. i sat down at gate B6 and plugged into the free USB port built into the armrest. 20 minutes. that's it

nothing happened. no popup. no notification. phone charged and i went home

two weeks later Chase calls me. suspicious wire transfer. $8,200 to an account i've never heard of. i open Zelle, two more. $2,400 on the 12th. $1,800 on the 17th. all three went through. all three had my 2FA codes

i couldn't figure out how. i have authenticator apps. i don't click links. i don't download random shit. my passwords are all unique

i plugged my iPhone into my MacBook and ran grok on the full device backup

the first thing it found made me put my phone down

a hidden MDM profile. mobile device management, the same system companies use to control work phones. remote camera. remote mic. screen recording. location tracking. full access to messages, photos, contacts, browser history. and a rogue root certificate that intercepted every HTTPS connection on my phone

it was called "AirPort Free Wi-Fi." it installed itself silently through the USB cable at the airport. no permission screen. no popup. nothing. just slid right in

server: https://t.co/ypwrOPtkKm
location: Chisinau, Moldova
domain age: 4 months
WHOIS: privacy-protected

19 days active. 847 commands executed on my phone. 612 location pings, one every 15 minutes. they mapped my apartment. my office. my daughter's school. my entire daily routine for almost three weeks

94 screenshots pulled from my phone. my Chase balance. my iMessage threads. my gmail password reset screens. my authenticator app with the codes on display. they didn't need to hack anything. they just watched my screen and used the codes before i could

4,291 photos exported. 1,247 contacts. 2,840 URLs from my browser history

the part that hit me the hardest was the location data. they had my daughter's school pinpointed by day 3. they knew what time i dropped her off and picked her up. every day for 19 days

$12,400. three transactions. all approved with 2FA codes they screenshotted off my phone in real time. by the time Chase flagged it the money was already in Moldova

i didn't get hacked by clicking a link. i didn't download malware. i plugged my phone into a USB port at an airport to charge it while i waited for my flight

what i did that night:

> removed the MDM profile and the rogue root certificate
> changed every password from my wife's laptop, not from my phone
> froze all cards, disputed all three transactions
> called the bank and put verbal verification on wire transfers
> filed a police report and an FTC complaint
> ordered a $12 USB data blocker off amazon. that's all it would have taken

my wife asked me why i was up at 3am. i showed her the grok output. she didn't say anything for about ten minutes. then she asked if they had photos of our daughter. they did. 4,291 of them

check your phone right now. settings > general > VPN & device management. if there is anything there you don't recognize, screenshot it and remove it immediately

don't ever plug your phone into a USB port you don't own. not at the airport. not at the hotel. not at the coffee shop. bring a wall adapter. bring a power bank. a USB cable is not just power. it's a data connection straight into your phone

🚨 ALLEGED CON ARTIST: Who is Louise Lucas? 

Let me share with you the backstory on a self-described "greedy" lawmaker who waged a war on merit, denigrating Asian American parents and families, and is now indicted for illegally selling marijuana and cheating to create "generational wealth" 

The text that indicts Virginia state Sen. Louise Lucas in a new Justice Department indictment announced by US Attorney General Todd Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel against her for alleged money laundering is this one:

💰 “this is our last chance at generational wealth . . . I’ve got too old to not be greedy.”

The words she allegedly later said: 
💰 “I got to get the license and I got to get the money rolling because I want — I want to make generation, create some generational wealth.”

Lucas is an important window into the choices that everyone faces: whether to advance in life through merit or through cheating. 

Read our coverage of the indictment here: 

'FOR PEOPLE WHO LOOK LIKE ME'
I know the day that I learned the name of Virginia state Sen. Louise Lucas: Feb. 18, 2021. 

WATCH the video I've shared her to see Lucas in action.

She was supporting Virginia state Sen. Scott Surovell and other Democratic lawmakers as they waged a wider battle to remove merit-based admissions to America's former No. 1 high school, Thomas Jefferson High School for Science and Technology, and other governor schools. Their bill: HB 2305.

There were some 20 mostly immigrant parents waiting to speak in the online waiting room: parents from India, China and elsewhere, who saw merit as the only path they have to realizing the American Dream and maybe if they were lucky creating "generational wealth."

Lucas wouldn't let the parents speak. I was watching the debate from the waiting room. My son was attending the school at the time, and I was writing about the efforts of parents to challenge the new admissions policy, eliminating the merit admissions test, as racist. 

A federal judge Conrad Hilton later supported the parents and the Coalition for TJ and called the new admissions policy "patently unconsitutional" and racist.

The ruling was overturned on appeal and the US Supreme Court wouldn't hear the appeal but is now set to hear a similar case from Montgomery County, Md.

Then-state Sen. Chap Petersen was opposing that effort as an effort to target the school's mostly Asian American student population. 

As Petersen spoke about TJ, he noted, “Its population is 80 percent minority.”

Lucas, who is black, interrupted him and said, “Sen. Petersen, for people who look like me, I would appreciate it if you would put a better definition to minority, because I know you’re not talking about people who look like me, so could you please, please be more specific?”

Petersen, whose wife is Korean American woman, said: “The population is about 70 percent Asian.”

Then he added: “People who look like my kids. My kids.” 

Lucas responded: "Mm-hmm."

The war on merit succeeded and TJHSST has plummeted in academic standards and national rankings and is now the FORMER No. 1 high school. Current Virginia Lt. Governor Ghazala Hashmi demonized "parents" and alleged they were racist and supported Lucas and Surovell. 

When Lucas lost the vote, she said: "We will overcome one day."

🔗 This is the full 2018 debate for anyone who wants to see Lucas and her war on merit: https://t.co/w7iGZqXnnW

FAST FORWARD: "GREED" vs. MERIT
Federal prosecutors allege one Lucas, used her political office as part of a years-long operation to sell marijuana, launder the proceeds — and ultimately turn Virginia’s legalization of recreational marijuana into what she allegedly called “generational wealth," not through merit but by allegedly cheating the system.

The 45-page federal indictment names names: 
❌ Louise Lucas
❌ Her daughter Lisa Lucas-Burke
❌ Her daughter Theresa Lucas-Lamb
❌ Her grandson Ryan Eichelberger
❌ Businessman Prince Albert William Hudson III 
❌ Businessman Carlton Upton Jr.
❌ Businesswoman Tameka Johnson

Prosecutors allege the “Lucas Enterprise” operated from at least 2019 -- two years before the debate on merit -- and pursued two intertwined objectives: 
❌ Distributing marijuana
❌ Using Lucas’ political influence to shape Virginia marijuana policy and obtain valuable recreational licenses

Here is the extraordinary chronology prosecutors laid out, in their own words. 

RISE TO POWER
Lucas was elected to the Virginia Senate in 1991 and rose to become chair of the powerful Senate Finance and Appropriations Committee and Senate President Pro Tempore.

According to the indictment, her family operated The Cannabis Outlet in Portsmouth.

💰 Her daughter Lisa Lucas-Burke allegedly handled business affairs and attended meetings.
💰 Her daughter Theresa Lucas-Lamb allegedly managed the store.
💰 Grandson Ryan Eichelberger allegedly worked in its day-to-day operations.

Prosecutors say Lucas was explicitly warned.

After a senior law-enforcement officer was hired in 2022, the indictment says he warned Lucas that selling marijuana was illegal and “was going to get her in trouble one day.”

At another meeting, the officer allegedly asked why, “given that she was a state senator and a wealthy woman,” she would engage in criminal behavior.

According to prosecutors, Lucas didn't answer.

By then, prosecutors allege marijuana was already moving through the family business.

2022: 'FREEDOM IS DOPE'
In early 2022, prosecutors say an alleged supplier identified ICC #1 contributed $15,000 to the 420ish Unity Festival, partly organized by Lucas.

The receipt allegedly described the payment as:

“Freedom is Dope.”

Then, on April 19, 2022, Lucas and daughter Lisa Lucas-Burke allegedly met ICC #1 at Lucas’ office.

The indictment says that between June and July 2022, an alleged supplier identified as ICC #1 delivered between THREE AND FIVE POUNDS of marijuana to The Cannabis Outlet.

Lucas allegedly paid between $3,500 and $4,000 IN CASH.

'VIRGINIA FREEDOM LIFE'
According to the indictment, Lucas asked ICC #1 whether he was a member of law enforcement before discussing marijuana prices.

That same day, daughter Lucas-Burke allegedly wrote a $6,600 check to ICC #1 from Virginia Freedom Life.

It bounced.

Lucas allegedly replaced it with another $6,600 check from Backyard Entertainment.

By fall 2022, prosecutors allege the business was operating at scale.

Between fall 2022 and early 2023, ICC #2 allegedly sold The Cannabis Outlet “multi-pound quantities of marijuana totaling approximately 100 pounds” for $100,000-$150,000.

Prosecutors say Lucas, through daughter Theresa Lucas-Lamb, paid $52,000 in checks and the remainder IN CASH.

Then came the texts.

'THE LUCAS LADIES'
On Oct. 3, 2022, prosecutors say Lucas texted the alleged supplier:

“Good morning … this is to confirm the time for our meeting at the store today. I am so excited and looking forward to seeing you”

And:

“we (The Lucas Ladies) love doing business with you”

'I'M GOING TO NEED MORE FLOWER'
Daughter Theresa Lucas-Lamb allegedly texted with the supplier about the mechanics of marijuana sales.

One message described packaging and selling “half ounces (14)” and “ounces (28).”

Another allegedly said:

“you can keep going on the blend if you can’t keep up with sativa and indica.”

Days later:

“Good morning. I’m going to need more flower.”

The money trail continued.

The indictment lists payment after payment from The Cannabis Outlet to Prince Albert William Hudson III, whom prosecutors describe as a marijuana supplier.

💰 December 2023: more than $21,000.
💰 January 2024: more than $26,000.
💰 February: more than $29,000.
💰 March: $129,000.
💰 April: $132,000.
💰 May: $125,000.
💰 June: $123,000.
💰 July: more than $79,000.
💰 August: $91,000.
💰 September: $67,000.

And investigators weren't merely watching.

💰 On Oct. 4, 2024, and Oct. 18, 2024, the indictment says law enforcement made CONTROLLED PURCHASES of marijuana from The Cannabis Outlet.

More controlled buys followed.

💰 On May 5, 2025, an undercover officer allegedly bought 10.2 grams of marijuana from The CBD Shoppe.

💰 By 2025, prosecutors allege payments continued flowing to Hudson and another alleged supplier, ICC #1.

The indictment records tens of thousands of dollars month after month.

Meanwhile, daughter Theresa Lucas-Lamb allegedly received a series of $2,500 payments from an Agri-Carter account controlled by Hudson.

Then investigators intercepted a shipment.

On Aug. 13, 2025, Norfolk police seized SEVEN POUNDS OF MARIJUANA allegedly shipped to High-N-Wellness in Norfolk.

According to prosecutors, payments and marijuana transactions nevertheless continued.

By October 2025, law enforcement was buying directly from The Cannabis Outlet again.

💰 Oct. 23, 2025: controlled purchase of ½ ounce.
💰 Oct. 31, 2025: controlled purchase of one ounce.

During that transaction, prosecutors say Eichelberger told the undercover officer another load of “product” was due Nov. 3.

'THE ELECTION' 
Then came a text prosecutors put directly into the indictment.

On Nov. 15, 2025, Lucas allegedly wrote about “the election” and told ICC #2:

“you know I will be carrying the legislation as the Chief Co-patron.”

She allegedly proposed sitting down to discuss “how about we begin with you sending at least a good faith payment of the money you owe me…”

'LIST OF STUFF FOR YOU TO TRY'
In January 2026, prosecutors say the operation moved directly into Lucas’ legislative office.

Grandson Ryan Eichelberger allegedly began texting businesswoman Tameka Johnson asking for “a lil have a list of stuff for you to try & get for next time.”

Then: “can you get the COAs for the flower and other products?”

💰 On Jan. 30, 2026, according to prosecutors, Lucas asked ICC #2 to come to her office at the Capitol complex in Richmond.

💰 There, the indictment says Lucas provided “partial repayment” of money ICC #2 had paid for an interest in Mama’s Chicken, LLC.

💰 Then Lucas allegedly asked ICC #2 to provide marijuana “samples.”

💰 The next day, Jan. 31, 2026, prosecutors say Lucas and ICC #2 met AGAIN — this time at her legislative office in Portsmouth.

Lucas allegedly called in daughter Lisa Lucas-Burke and grandson Ryan Eichelberger.

They discussed sources of marijuana.

When Eichelberger asked whether the cannabis was hemp, prosecutors say ICC #2 replied:

“[I]t’s not hemp, it’s THC.”

'GET GENERATIONAL WEALTH'
Then prosecutors allege Lucas explained the endgame.

After the conversation, Lucas and ICC #2 allegedly continued discussing marijuana and marijuana licensing.

According to the indictment, Lucas said obtaining a license was a way for her to:

“get generational wealth and this is my last chance.”

The alleged undercover operation kept going.

💰 Feb. 3, 2026: ICC #1 allegedly arrived at The Cannabis Outlet with “a large bag” from his vehicle and took it inside.

💰 Feb. 5, 2026: controlled purchase of 69.5 grams from The CBD Shoppe.

💰 Same day: controlled purchase of 116 grams from High-N-Wellness.

💰 On Feb. 9, 2026, prosecutors say Lucas called ICC #2 and discussed the recreational-marijuana legislation pending in the General Assembly.

The indictment quotes Lucas:

“this is our last chance at generational wealth . . . I’ve got too old to not be greedy.”

Two days later, law enforcement allegedly observed ICC #2 throwing a white trash bag into a dumpster.

Investigators recovered it.

The indictment says the bag contained marijuana packaging bearing “the odor of marijuana.”

March 2026: prosecutors allege the political and business sides increasingly converged.

Lucas allegedly told grandson Eichelberger and businesswoman Tameka Johnson to find additional marijuana sources.

Then, prosecutors say, Lucas telephoned another Virginia legislator and explained why she needed a marijuana license.

The alleged quote is stunning:

“I got to get the license and I got to get the money rolling because I want — I want to make generation, create some generational wealth.”

She allegedly continued:

“I need to be covered under his (UPTON’s) um, hemp license.”

On March 11, 2026. prosecutors say Lucas participated in another call with Virginia legislators and daughter Lisa Lucas-Burke about recreational marijuana licenses.

Lucas allegedly said:

“we trying to disqualify somebody [UCC #2] until he pays me back my money.”

March 31, 2026: Businessman Carlton Upton Jr. allegedly met Lucas at her Portsmouth office.

According to the indictment, Upton told Lucas:

“I only got five licenses, but you know what I mean, you first, so I need to talk to you before I make any decisions that affect you.”

💰 April 23, 2026: prosecutors say Lucas called a member of the Virginia Cannabis Control Authority and asked whether there was anything the official could do for her.

💰 According to the indictment, Lucas said she needed “to invest in something that — that can help me generate some uh, generational wealth for my family.”

Then came the raids.

💰 May 6, 2026: Federal search warrant at The Cannabis Outlet — marijuana recovered.
💰 Federal search warrant at The CBD Shoppe — marijuana recovered.
💰 Federal search warrant at Hudson’s Exotic World in Danville — marijuana recovered.
💰 July 10, 2026: Law enforcement returned to The Cannabis Outlet for another controlled purchase.
💰 Agents bought two strains labeled “Sativa” and “Indica.” According to the indictment: Both tested positive for marijuana.

The grand jury ultimately charged an alleged racketeering conspiracy involving Lucas, daughter Lisa Lucas-Burke, businessman Prince Albert William Hudson III, grandson Ryan Eichelberger, daughter Theresa Lucas-Lamb and businessman Carlton Upton Jr.

Prosecutors say the alleged enterprise sought to obtain and illegally distribute marijuana AND procure “generational wealth” for its members.

The indictment goes further.

Prosecutors allege the enterprise used business entities to disguise marijuana proceeds and used Lucas’ political influence “to insulate the Lucas Enterprise from state law enforcement actions.”

They also allege her influence was used to pursue marijuana licenses that could financially benefit the enterprise.

Prosecutors describe Lucas as the alleged “leader of the enterprise.”

They accuse her of approving and directing criminal activities, arranging marijuana acquisition and distribution, supervising laundering of marijuana proceeds and using her political influence in an effort to shape Virginia legislation for herself and her family.

The indictment contains EIGHT COUNTS, including allegations involving:

❌ Racketeering conspiracy
❌ Conspiracy to distribute and possess with intent to distribute marijuana
❌ Money laundering conspiracy
❌ Honest-services fraud conspiracy
❌ Maintaining drug-involved premises
❌ Possession of a firearm in furtherance of a drug-trafficking crime
❌ Wire fraud

The charges vary by defendant.

One of the most consequential allegations isn't simply that marijuana was illegally sold.

Prosecutors allege Lucas used her elected office to advance the financial interests of herself, her family and associates as Virginia debated creation of a potentially lucrative recreational marijuana market.

The honest-services count alleges a scheme to deprive Virginians of Lucas’ “intangible right” to her honest services.

The indictment alleges Lucas invested money with ICC #2 in an entity positioned to benefit from marijuana licensing, did not report that interest on required Statements of Economic Interests, and later demanded a partial $100,000 repayment while continuing to work to direct a license to ICC #2.

These are allegations. An indictment is not proof of guilt, and every defendant is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty. 

That's the position that Sen. Surovell, the lawmaker who pushed the legislation to remove merit from Virginia's No. 1 high school, is taking as he stands by her in support against the indictments.

The government has now laid out, in extraordinary detail, its theory of how an alleged marijuana business, a family network, money and political power converged over years.

And prosecutors repeatedly return to the phrases they attribute to Lucas herself: creating "generational wealth" by being "greedy."

I hope the telling of this story will give you a wider window into why this case captures not only the crossroads that a politician faces of success through merit or through cheating but also the questions that a nation faces: to go down the path that this lawmaker allegedy supported of shortcuts and dishonor or to choose a path of honor, merit and hard work. 

In 2021, Lucas silenced parents who believed in merit and hard work.

text:
Last night IFF, @SFLCin and @geoblockedindia received a legal notice said to be issued purportedly on behalf of the RSS. It’s hard to believe this comes from an organisation that has had a century to practise its paperwork and hence this may even be a weird prank! This notice asks us to stop criticising the Government’s blocking orders and stop documenting them. It also wants us to confirm in writing within seven days (seriously).

We can tell it’s an excellent teaching aid and here are seven lessons from it.

1) Say who you are: The notice names no advocate and gives no enrollment number. It is signed by an “Authorised Signatory” with no name. Replies go to a free Proton Mail ID, and the “office” is a residential flat in outer Delhi. A notice that can’t tell you who sent it is less a legal document than a weather event.

2) Have a grievance of your own: It never says how its client is harmed when we criticise a MeitY advisory. It complains on behalf of the Government’s blocking orders. The Union has no shortage of lawyers, and it hasn’t asked for volunteers.

3) Name the law: It threatens “appropriate legal action” under “the applicable provisions of law” and doesn’t cite a single section of any statute. A threat with no law, is literally an empty threat.

4) Don’t ask people to give up a fundamental right within seven days: The first demand is that we stop “publicly opposing” government directions. In Shreya Singhal (2015), the Supreme Court held that discussion and advocacy of a cause, however unpopular, sit at the heart of Article 19(1)(a). Opposing an order is how its legality gets tested. That is the Constitution working as intended.

5) Check whether the courts asked for the thing you want stopped” In Anuradha Bhasin (2020), the Supreme Court held that orders restricting fundamental rights must be made available so people can challenge them. The Reddit order is on the public Lumen Database because Reddit put it there. Reading a public database and saying what’s in it has a name. It’s called research.

6) Show us the spark and the powder keg: The notice says our work weakens national security measures, but it gives no instance, date or harm. In S. Rangarajan (1989), the Supreme Court held that the danger feared from speech can’t be remote, conjectural or far-fetched. It has to be like a spark in a powder keg. A post about a Lumen filing is not a spark.

7) Read it once more before you press send: The paragraphs run 1, then an empty 2 and 3, then 4. A PIN code wanders into the facts. The account it targets is on “Twitter”. 

Our reply is short. The notice is legally deficient because it makes no material allegation and cites no illegality. We will respectfully continue to advance constitutional rights, as we have done before. Notices like this rarely expect to win in court. They expect the recipient to get tired. We often are tired, but it has never changed what we do. Solidarity with @SFLCin and @geoblockedindia. 

If your post or account has been blocked in India, write to legal@internetfreedom.in.

text:
I have my twitter back. 

It took me 6 days, a cyber police complaint and a legal notice to twitter to recover my account. 

If you got a DM from me last week asking you to vote for me for a podcast, that was not me. Please don't click it & If you already did, please change your password ASAP.

Here's what happened:

→I received a late night DM from a friend to vote on a podcast which redirected me to a a login page that looked right, and I typed in my password (classic)

→The attacker logged in and changed my 2FA within minutes & I was locked out of my account. (I still don't understand how my email and phone number were changed. Neither my email nor my phone was compromised.)

→Then he used account to DM followers a fake "vote for me" link. Each person who clicks becomes the next account sending it. That is how these spread.

What didn't work:

→ I filed X's hacked account form within the hour. Less than two hours later, the reply came: X could not verify me as the account owner. Their suggestion was to create a new account. Once 2FA is changed, the automated system treats the attacker as the real owner.

→ So I went to the Grievance Officer. Under the IT Rules, 2021, X must appoint a Resident Grievance Officer in India. He has no email address. X does not accept legal notices by email. 

The only options are a web form or post to their physical office.

Here's what worked:

→First, a cyber complaint on https://t.co/Uzds8BObDW (or call 1930).

→Second, a legal notice to the Grievance Officer. Under the IT Rules, impersonation complaints must be acted on within 24 hours.

→Third, the same notice sent by registered post, and to every X email address I could find.

The notice put X on record. It set out the ticket number, the phishing link, and the cyber complaint number. It showed proof of ownership: the registered email, the phone number, and the Premium subscription paid from my card. It ended with a clear ask and a deadline.

Six days after the hack, I was back in.

If this happens to you:
• Act within hours
• File X's hacked account form from your registered email and be persistent (this is important)
• File at https://t.co/Uzds8BObDW and keep the acknowledgement
• Notice to the Grievance Officer via the https://t.co/YkDfcMQwzE form and by post
